## Surfaced by the #789 test-coverage round (2026-08-31)

Found while writing the coverage in [decisions §§ 807-814](../architecture/decisions.md). These are the ones that need their own change rather than being closed in that round.

- [x] **`check_production_env` and `env_isolation` are off the required gate.** Closed 2026-09-01 ([decisions § 862](../architecture/decisions.md) – [§ 866](../architecture/decisions.md)). Both suites now run in an `env-isolation` job inside `ci.yml`, named in the `CI gate`'s `needs:`; `env-isolation.yml` is deleted, `env-example-scan` came with them as a third step of the same job, and the path filter is deliberately not reproduced (every step is stdlib-only and install-free, so two jobs became one and the fold gives a runner slot back). **The filing's "both" was one item and a half.** `env_isolation.mjs` is a vite plugin, recorded under `NOT_A_GUARD`, not `OFF_THE_GATE`; `check_production_env.mjs` was the single entry, and it does not go — its CLI asserts about a RELEASE env, and `build-web` compiles against `placeholder.supabase.co`, the value the guard exists to refuse, so the only ci.yml form available was an inverted `if node …; then fail; fi` that would also pass when the guard CRASHED (§ 741's shape). Its reason is rewritten instead, which is the other half of the point: the old one had become false. **What was actually missing was a rule, not an entry.** The census asked only that a guard's suite be run by SOME workflow, so this state satisfied it for its whole life; it now has to be run by `ci.yml` or be named in `SUITE_OFF_THE_GATE` with a reason ([§ 863](../architecture/decisions.md)), which is one entry. The fold also closed a hole nobody had filed: the scan reads `apps/watch_ios/WatchApp/SupabaseService.swift`, which `.gitleaks.toml` allowlists whole and no filter path matched, so on a PR a live key pasted there was read by nothing ([§ 866](../architecture/decisions.md)).
- [x] **Three mobile dotenv gates read `dotenv.env[...]` with no try/catch, where their sibling fails closed.** **CLOSED 2026-08-31** ([§ 822](../architecture/decisions.md)). The filing got the framing right and every specific wrong. Right: `main.dart` loads dotenv before `runApp` unconditionally, so an uninitialised read is unreachable in the app; and the asymmetry was real and worth closing. Wrong: none of the three named gates was missing a guard. `offRouteEscalationEnabled` and `adaptiveFitnessGateEnabled` are pure `String? → bool` parsers that never touch dotenv and cannot throw — the reads are at their call sites, and all five of those guarded already, three with `try/catch` and two with `dotenv.isInitialized &&` (equivalent: `NotInitializedError` is the only thing `dotenv.env` throws). `_weighInGate` has had its `try/catch` since `71a255845`. What was actually wrong is the *binding*: key plus guard spelled at five call sites in two idioms, two of them duplicates, and two of them private top-level getters inside screen files — so the test the filing asked for could not be written. Each flag now owns one binding module (`off_route_flag.dart` / `adaptive_fitness_flag.dart` / `weigh_in_flag.dart`, beside the existing `nearby_flag.dart`, mirroring web's `*_flag.ts` layer), the parse stays in its parity-pair file, and `env_flag_test.dart` pins all four answering `false` against an uninitialised dotenv plus a guard that a gate key read literally outside its own module fails the suite.
- [x] **Two waits in `nutrition_screen_test.dart` are measured vacuous.** **CLOSED 2026-09-02** ([decisions § 990](../architecture/decisions.md)). Re-measured with an instrumented `pumpUntil`: both spent **0** loop turns, exactly as filed. The reason it was left standing — that `pumpUntil` cannot drive a route transition under the fake clock, so a predicate about the picker risks a timeout — is right about the picker and wrong about the wait: what is being waited on is a real file write, and the `OfflineSyncStore` entry file under the fake `path_provider` root is observable without the dialog's pop completing. Both predicates now read the disk (`meal_templates/` and `recipes/`); measured 5 turns each afterwards, and pointing the helper at a directory nothing writes makes both time out naming what they wait for. The `pumpAndSettle` that follows still does the route work. Every other `pumpUntil` in the file was measured in the same pass — all nine spend at least one turn. "The saved template/recipe to appear in the picker" spends zero loop turns: `find.text` matches the dialog's own `EditableText`, so the predicate is already true before the save. It is [§ 723](../architecture/decisions.md)'s class, and it survived that round's sweep. Left in place deliberately for now — `pumpUntil` cannot wait on a route transition under the fake clock, so every correct predicate risks a timeout instead, and the `store.rows.length == 2` wait that follows does spin and does cover the behaviour. Closing it means a predicate that can distinguish the dialog's text from the picker's, or a different wait primitive for route transitions.
- [x] **`LocalRunStore` and `LocalRouteStore` carry the same unserialised delete-vs-write shape [§ 821](../architecture/decisions.md) closed on `OfflineSyncStore`.** **CLOSED** 2026-08-31 — [§ 828](../architecture/decisions.md) + [§ 829](../architecture/decisions.md). The filing was right about the shape, the outcome and the reason it was worth its own slice, and it under-counted its own evidence twice. Its headline said twelve atomic-write call sites outside `OfflineSyncStore` while its own breakdown adds to **fourteen** (7 + 5 + 2); twelve is the count for the two stores it names in the title. The route-store outcome it measured reproduces exactly — a `delete` against an in-flight `save` is silently dropped, memory *and* disk keep the row, and a cold load keeps it too — and the run store does the same plus re-writes the index the delete had just pruned. What it missed is the sidecars, which are the worse half: `route_owner_tags.json` is read-modify-write with a `_ownerTagsTouched` ledger cleared by whichever write lands first, so eight overlapping `save` calls left as few as **two of eight** routes tagged, and an untagged route is drainable into another account on a shared device ([§ 67](../architecture/decisions.md)) — reproducible about one run in three. `watch_ingest_queue.dart` was taken too (the entry's own closing sentence names three stores): `setLastKnownOwner` is fired unawaited from both `main.dart` call sites, and its clear-vs-stamp race reproduces every time. And the `FileLock` the filing flagged "worth checking on the way past" turned out to exclude nothing at all — POSIX record locks are owned by the process, so two handles in one process, including the WorkManager isolate the lock named, both acquire (§ 829); it is gone, its `.lock` residue is swept, and an arch guard fails the suite if either store spells it again. § 821's chain fit and was lifted into `serialiseStoreWrite` in `core_models`, made re-entrant so a shared persist helper cannot deadlock behind its own caller. The recording path is deliberately **outside** it — pinned by a test that holds the chain open through a never-completed `Completer` and asserts a tick still lands.
- [x] **`gym_detail_visibility_test.dart` prints a `PathNotFoundException` on the double-tap case.** **CLOSED 2026-08-31** ([§ 821](../architecture/decisions.md)). The filing got the exception shape and the L4 catch right, and the diagnosis backwards on both halves. It is **in the test**, not in shared store logic: `persist` installs the row in `rowsById` synchronously, so the visibility chip flips a frame before the atomic write lands, `pumpUntil` returned on it, and the temp-directory teardown then deleted that write's `.tmp` out from under its rename — nothing to do with the double tap (the `_actionBusy` guard holds, `updateCalls` is 1) and equally reachable from the single-tap case. And the temp path has been unique per write since `writeStringAtomic` shipped, so the collision the filing implies could not happen. The test now waits on the file, which also pins the offline-first durability the chip was wrongly credited with proving. **But the family the filing was reaching for is real, and two members were measured in production code**: `clear()` (the sign-out wipe) deletes every file in the directory including the `.tmp` of an in-flight write, producing exactly that `PathNotFoundException`; and a delete that overtakes an in-flight write to the same id leaves the row's file back on disk with `rowsById` saying it is gone, resurrecting it at the next cold-load with no exception at all. Both are fixed by serialising every directory-mutating entry point on one chain keyed on the directory, and both are pinned by tests that fail on the old path.
- [x] **CLOSED 2026-08-31** ([decisions § 815](../architecture/decisions.md)) — **The 23 `handler_envelope.test.ts` integration tests are still outside every mutation operator.** Closed with the entry it restates, in the § 815 round. The 785 / 0 / 0 figure it cites was exact and still is; the 23 was deno's ignored count and the runnable set was 22 (23 now, with the verify-token case § 815 added). The fix shape it proposed — "a neutered SERVED tree between the boot step and the test step" — was the right half and the wrong operator: a blanket neuter proves only that each case notices a dead function, which is the weaker claim § 788 already makes about the other 785, and it would have found none of the three non-discriminating cases that a per-gate mutation with declared spares did.

## Surfaced by the #789 test-coverage round 28 (2026-09-01)

Found while writing the coverage in [decisions §§ 832-851](../architecture/decisions.md). Reported rather than half-fixed: each needs its own change, and two of them need a decision before any code.

- [x] **`catalogue_browse`'s accent fold diverges between web and mobile, and the parity registry cannot see it.** Closed 2026-09-01 ([decisions § 852](../architecture/decisions.md) through § 856). The entry understated it by counting only letters and only what the web `\p{Diacritic}` strip reaches: measured by dumping BOTH folds over every Unicode scalar value and diffing them, **14,719 code points folded differently, 13,746 of them letters** — the 1,443 the entry names, plus all 11,172 Hangul syllables (web decomposes them to jamo), the 1,002 CJK compatibility ideographs, and 466 code points Dart's own `toLowerCase` leaves uppercase because its case tables are older than the web's (the Georgian Mtavruli capitals, Cherokee, Osage, Adlam). The table is now GENERATED — `scripts/gen_catalogue_fold_table.mjs` derives it from the Unicode data Node carries and emits `apps/mobile_android/lib/catalogue_fold_table.dart`, 4,420 entries, the shape `age_grade_tables.dart` already models — and it carries the case mapping too, so the Dart fold no longer depends on the runtime's Unicode version. Hangul is computed rather than tabled (its decomposition is arithmetic; the generator asserts the arithmetic reproduces NFD for all 11,172). One thing had to move on web first: `toLowerCase` implements the Final_Sigma rule, which made U+03A3 the ONLY code point in Unicode whose fold depended on its neighbours — measured across every scalar value in three contexts — so web now collapses `ς` onto `σ`, a WIDENING that also fixes a real defect there (`οδοσ` did not reach `ΟΔΟΣ`). Two guards, because the two halves are different claims: `check_catalogue_fold_table.mjs` compares the committed table with a fresh render (and names an ICU bump apart from a hand-edit), and `catalogue_fold_table.test.ts` runs the SHIPPED web `fold` against that table. 14 mirror vectors each side, 12 of which the old table answered differently. The deliberate residual is canonical REORDERING — two adjacent surviving marks in non-canonical order, which no normalised text can be — stated in both doc comments and in § 856. Original entry: **`catalogue_browse`'s accent fold diverges between web and mobile on 1,443 letters, and the parity registry cannot see it.** Web folds with `normalize('NFD')` + `\p{Diacritic}` strip, which reaches every canonically-decomposable letter in Unicode; the Dart twin spells the class out as a 19-entry table because Dart's core library has no normalisation, and that table stops at Latin Extended-A. Measured over the BMP, **1,443 letters are de-accented by web and left intact by mobile**: all 245 of Latin Extended Additional (the Vietnamese set — `Đèo Hải Vân` folds to `deo hai van` on web and `đeo hải van` on mobile), 340 Greek across both blocks, 57 Cyrillic, 91 Latin Extended-B including the pinyin tone letters (`ǎ`, `ǐ`), Vietnamese `Ơ`/`Ư`, and 7 spacing diacritics inside Latin-1 itself (`´`, `¨`, `¯`, `¸`, `·`, `` ` ``, `^`) that web deletes outright. Two consequences, both real: a reader typing `hai` reaches the segment on web and not on the phone, and `byName` compares folded names, so **the catalogue sorts differently on the two platforms**. The doc comment on the Dart side is accurate about *why* it is a table and silent about *how far* the table reaches. `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` compares the two registries, not the two behaviours, so nothing fails. The durable fix is the one `age_grade_tables.dart` already models — **generate** the table from NFD rather than hand-maintaining it, commit it, and guard it against the generator — not to narrow web to match, which would delete working behaviour. The letters with no canonical decomposition (`ø`, `đ`, `ł`, `ß`, `æ`, …) must stay out of it either way: web keeps them too, and folding them would invent an equivalence NFD does not have.
- [x] **If Supabase Cloud ships storage-api's `protect_objects_delete` trigger, the export sweep silently stops deleting anything.** Closed 2026-09-01 ([decisions § 857](../architecture/decisions.md)) — **measured, and it is not a forward risk.** CLI 2.84.2 (CI's pin) starts storage-api **v1.44.11** and CLI 2.109.1 (the workstation) starts **v1.62.5**; `0055-prevent-direct-deletes.sql` is in **both**, so the trigger is on CI too and the escape GUC the § 839 test set was load-bearing there, not a no-op. It is also **statement-level**, so it fires on a DELETE matching no rows: the nightly job has been raising every night whether or not anything was stale, and because the DELETE precedes `expire_stale_export_jobs()` no `data_export_jobs` row was expired either. `20270703000002` sets `storage.allow_delete_query` transaction-locally — the precedent `20260927_001`'s orphan cleanup already set — and counts the stale objects surviving its own DELETE, raising if any do: a delete FILTERED rather than refused reports zero through `get diagnostics` and used to go on to mark the row `expired` while the archive was still there. The fixture no longer hands the function the GUC, so the suite drives the escape rather than supplying it. The one thing that remains is an owner call, filed below.
- [x] **`check_shared_constants.mjs` reads the migration text for the photo buckets' mime lists, which is a different claim from what the applied row says.** Closed 2026-09-01 ([decisions § 858](../architecture/decisions.md)). **Both rails kept — they make different claims and neither subsumes the other:** the script compares the migration text against `STRIPPABLE_IMAGE_MIME_TYPES` and `kStrippableImageMimeTypes`, which is four source files agreeing with each other and which no SQL assertion can reach; pgtap reads the applied `storage.buckets` rows, which no source read can. The applied-row assertions are held over a DERIVED population — every bucket accepting any `image/` type — so a fifth image bucket is held to § 557 the day it appears rather than the day someone extends a list of four names, they carry the null arm the old `@>`/`<@` filter silently excluded (`null @> array[…]` is null, so a bucket that lost its allowlist dropped out of its own check), and `image/heic` / `image/heif` are now named outright across every bucket. The source rail was hardened in the same change: it compares under `match: 'all'`, which has no key coverage check, so a bucket it failed to resolve simply stopped being compared while the other three still agreed — both that and a statement assigning the column in a shape it cannot read (which it used to skip, reporting the value from BEFORE the change) now throw.

## Surfaced by the #789 test-coverage round 29 (2026-09-01)

- [x] **Decide whether the export retention sweep should delete `storage.objects` rows at all, and measure what happens to the bytes when it does.** Closed 2026-09-03 ([decisions § 1049](../architecture/decisions.md)) — **measured, and the belief is WRONG.** A 4 KiB `application/zip` probe uploaded through the real Storage API, aged past the seven-day window and swept by the shipped `cleanup_stale_export_blobs()`, loses its `storage.objects` row (the function reports 1, its post-condition passes, the object stops being listable) and its bytes stay on the storage backend with a **matching `sha256`**. Corroborating: the same volume held 74 files across every bucket against 0 rows, including 20 export archives nine days old that nothing has ever reaped; there is no `pg_cron` job touching storage bytes and the storage container runs one `node dist/start/server.js` and nothing else. The trigger says so itself — `Use the Storage API instead`, hint `This prevents accidental data loss from orphaned objects` — and the escape GUC removes the refusal without making a row delete into an object delete. **The decision: keep deleting the rows, and stop calling it retention.** Removing reachability is the part SQL can do and is strictly better than [§ 857](../architecture/decisions.md)'s predecessor state, which deleted nothing at all; but it is not an Art 17 erasure, and `docs/compliance/data-subject-rights.md` now says so instead of saying the bytes are reaped. Two limits on the claim: this is the local `file` backend, so what is proved is the MECHANISM (no database-side reaper exists; storage-api's own delete path is the only thing that removes a backend object), and confirming the residue on Cloud still means listing the bucket over the S3 endpoint. The structural fix is filed below rather than built: it needs a new value in `jobs_kind_chk`, a set-shaped CHECK whose coverage rule lives in `check_constraint_unions.mjs`, outside the backend lane. Original entry: [§ 857](../architecture/decisions.md) restored the sweep by setting storage-api's documented escape GUC, which is what `20260927_001`'s orphan-blob cleanup already does — but that trigger exists precisely because deleting the row is not deleting the object, and its own hint says so ("This prevents accidental data loss from orphaned objects"). `20260927_001` recorded the belief that "the actual blob bytes are reaped by the storage backend's background sweeper once the row is gone"; **that belief is stated nowhere else in this repo and was not measured.** If it is wrong, every Art 20 archive ever swept is still sitting in the object store, unreachable through the Storage API but not erased — a retention claim `docs/compliance/data-subject-rights.md` makes on our behalf. Measuring it needs a real project (list the bucket through the S3-compatible endpoint after a sweep), not more reading. The alternative shape is to move the sweep onto the Storage API — a job kind in the Go worker, which already writes the archive through that API and already holds the service key — leaving `expire_stale_export_jobs()` as the only SQL half. That is a structural change to a shipped retention path and to the cron schedule, which is why it was not taken with the fix: the fix restores a sweep that was deleting nothing at all, and it is strictly better than the state it replaced under either answer.

## Surfaced by the #789 test-coverage round 30, Wear OS tier (2026-09-02)

- [x] **`BODY_SENSORS_BACKGROUND` is declared in the Wear manifest and requested nowhere, so it can never be granted.** **CLOSED round 34 ([decisions § 1015](../architecture/decisions.md)) — by REMOVING the declaration, not by building the two-step flow this entry proposed.** The unrequestable half was confirmed exactly as filed. The premise underneath it was not: Google's Health Services permission table scopes `BODY_SENSORS_BACKGROUND` to `PassiveMonitoringClient`, gives `ExerciseClient` background access with no background permission at all, and lists `MeasureClient`'s background access as **no** — "not intended for background capture or workout tracking". `HeartRateMonitor` uses `MeasureClient`, so the permission was not the gate on this app's heart rate and granting it would have changed nothing about the ambient transition. The two-step request flow would have been correct in mechanism and inert in effect. `ManifestGuardsTest` now asserts the permission is ABSENT, carrying the measurement, so re-adding it fails until the client changes too. Two things the sweep found underneath it are separate entries: the recording service never started as a `health` foreground service at all ([§ 1016](../architecture/decisions.md)), and the ambient-HR capability itself needs `ExerciseClient` — filed below. Original text: Measured the same way [§ 881](../architecture/decisions.md) measured `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`: `AndroidManifest.xml` declares it (with a comment saying HR stops streaming once the display goes ambient without it, and that the Play Data Safety form lists it), and `grep -rn 'BODY_SENSORS_BACKGROUND' apps/watch_wear/**/*.kt` returns nothing — the only runtime request the app makes is `permissionLauncher.launch(...)` in `RunWatchApp.kt`, which asks for `ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION`, `BODY_SENSORS`, `ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION` and now `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`. It is registered as an exemption in `ManifestPermissionCoverageTest` rather than fixed, for a reason that is not scheduling: a **background** permission cannot ride the same request as its foreground half — Android requires a second request made only after `BODY_SENSORS` is granted, and bundling them gets the background one denied outright. So the fix is a two-step permission flow with its own UI state, and the thing it claims to fix — that Health Services keeps delivering `HEART_RATE_BPM` past the ambient transition on a Wear OS 3.5+ watch — is a platform behaviour no host-JVM test can observe and no emulator reproduces honestly (the emulator synthesises HR). It needs a real watch and a run long enough to dim. The visible symptom if the claim is right: `avg_bpm` on a long run reflects only the minutes the display was awake, which nothing on the wrist would report as an error.
- [x] **Denying location on the Wear pre-run screen is a silent no-op.** **CLOSED round 34 ([decisions § 1018](../architecture/decisions.md)).** Confirmed exactly as filed — the callback was two lines with no else — and the fix covers three more denials the same callback was absorbing: `BODY_SENSORS` (no heart rate), `ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION` (no step count) and `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` (no ongoing-run chip, the loss § 881 exists about). `permissionOutcome` grades the result map into `canStart` plus the ordered list of what was actually lost; `PermissionNotice` renders a sentence per entry plus ask-again, the app permission screen where the watch has one, and the written path. Ten new keys in all seven catalogues. The entry's reason for not fixing it — "a UI change, not a defect fix, and outside a coverage round's remit" — was the wrong call: a control that changes nothing is a defect. Original text: `RunWatchApp.kt`'s permission callback is `if (granted[ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION] == true) { showCountdown = true }` with no else branch, so a runner who taps GO and denies the prompt (or who denied it once before, after which the system may not prompt again) is returned to the pre-run screen unchanged — no message, no state change, no indication the tap did anything. The gate itself is correct and fail-closed; what is missing is the report. It is filed rather than fixed because the honest fix is a new user-visible string in all seven catalogues plus a decision about where it renders on a 46 mm screen that already carries a battery-saver chip, a sync chip, and a sign-in chip — a UI change, not a defect fix, and outside a coverage round's remit. The measurement is the two-line callback and the absent `else`.

## Surfaced by the #789 round 34 Wear OS sweep (2026-09-02)

Found sweeping `apps/watch_wear/` for one class — a platform capability the app
declares or requests whose failure path is silent. The population, the five
defects fixed and the negative results are in
[decisions §§ 1015-1020](../architecture/decisions.md). These four are what is
left: two need hardware, one needs a rewrite, one is a UI decision.

- [x] **Continuous heart rate on the wrist needs `ExerciseClient`, not a permission.** [§ 1015](../architecture/decisions.md) removed `BODY_SENSORS_BACKGROUND` after measuring that it gates `PassiveMonitoringClient` and that `MeasureClient` — what `HeartRateMonitor` uses — is documented as foreground-only and "not intended for background capture or workout tracking". So the symptom the removed permission claimed to fix is real and unaddressed: HR sampled through `MeasureClient` is not promised past the point the app stops being visible. The Wear OS answer for a workout is `ExerciseClient`, which the same table gives background access with **no** background permission, and which would also replace the app's own GPS + distance plumbing if taken whole. Scope it first: `ExerciseClient` owns the exercise state machine (`prepareExercise` / `startExercise` / auto-pause / laps) and would sit under, or replace, `RunRecordingService`'s own — so this is a recorder rewrite with a bench day at the end, not a client swap. What can be decided from source is that `MeasureClient` is the wrong client for a 12-hour ultra; what needs a watch is how much of the recorder should move. Scoped 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1054](../architecture/decisions.md); the code is deliberately unwritten and the scoping is the deliverable. `ExerciseClient` is confirmed the right client (1.1.0-rc02 is already a dependency, `minSdk` is already 30) and confirmed a recorder rewrite, not a client swap: it subsumes 1,455 lines across eight files pinned by 212 host-JVM tests in 16 files, none of which can drive Health Services. Three breaking edges decide the sequencing, and all three are about something OTHER than the runner deciding the run is over — `ExerciseTrackedStatus.OTHER_APP_IN_PROGRESS` means one owner per device (today the app records through Samsung Health / Fitbit / Fit; under `ExerciseClient` it could not, or would need the recorder kept as a fallback), `AUTO_ENDED` / `AUTO_ENDED_PERMISSION_LOST` let the platform end a run, and recovery inverts from `CheckpointStore` to a platform-owned exercise that outlives the process. None of the three is reproducible on the emulator, so it needs the bench day the sibling entry wants; the order is probe `getCapabilitiesAsync` on hardware, then move heart rate ALONE while GPS and distance stay ours, then decide whether the rest moves at all. Two candidate "small safe pieces" were considered and rejected on the record, one of which is filed below.
- [x] **Nothing on the wrist reports that heart rate is unavailable mid-run.** [§ 1017](../architecture/decisions.md) made every acquisition failure fail closed rather than crash — but `RunningScreen` renders the bpm line only when `bpm != null`, so "declined the permission", "watch has no HR sensor", "Health Services refused registration" and "sample not acquired yet" are one blank space. The pre-run notice ([§ 1018](../architecture/decisions.md)) covers the permission case at the moment the runner can act on it, which is the dominant one and the reason this is filed rather than fixed; the device cases it cannot cover. Doing it properly means `RecordingRepository.Metrics` carrying an HR-availability tri-state, the service publishing it from the `.catch` and from `onRegistrationFailed`, and one more caption on a 46 mm screen that already carries distance, pace, bpm, steps and lap count. Worth doing when someone has a watch to see the layout on. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1052](../architecture/decisions.md). Built as filed, with one correction to the shape: the caption reuses the slot the bpm reading occupies rather than adding a line, so the 46 mm layout is unchanged and the longest new string costs five characters against `146 bpm`. The root was `HeartRateMonitor.stream()` being a `Flow<Int>` — the monitor knew which of the four situations it was and discarded it one line later; it now emits `HeartRateUpdate(availability, bpm?)` and the service publishes it from both exits of its collector. Off-wrist is kept distinct from unavailable because it is the only one a runner can act on mid-run; the rest fold into one caption because none of them is. Found and fixed a second defect underneath: nothing ever cleared `bpm` once set, so a watch that slipped off the wrist at minute three rendered that figure for the rest of the run. Three strings in all seven catalogues; `HeartRateAvailabilityTest` pins the mapping against the SDK's own `DataTypeAvailability.VALUES` and fails if that list grows.
- [x] **`ActiveRunTileService.requestUpdate` is called unguarded from the recording path.** `RunRecordingService.startRecording` calls it inside `onStartCommand`, so a throw from `TileService.getUpdater(context)` on a build with no Tiles host would end the run the same way [§ 1017](../architecture/decisions.md)'s sensor streams did. Examined and deliberately left alone in that round: the updater is documented as best-effort, no failure of it has been observed, and adding a `try` on a hypothesis is the speculative-defence the house rules refuse. Recorded so the next reader knows it was looked at rather than missed. It becomes real the moment anyone sees a crash trace through `getUpdater`. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1053](../architecture/decisions.md), and the filed premise was **wrong in both directions**. Wrong first: `getUpdater` was decompiled out of `tiles-1.6.2.aar` and only allocates, and the no-Tiles-host case named here is the one case AndroidX already handles — `buildUpdateBindIntent` logs and returns null, `requestUpdateInternal` logs and returns, no throw. So a guard justified on THAT scenario would indeed have been speculative defence. Wrong second: the call site is a layering violation anyway, because `CompositeTileUpdateRequester.requestUpdate` iterates its two delegates with no catch between them and they make one unwrapped IPC call each (`Context.bindService`, which documents `SecurityException`, and `Context.sendBroadcast`). What settles it is position, not probability: the start-path call sits between publishing `Recording` and subscribing GPS, HR, steps, the ticker and the checkpoint job, and the service already wraps every other auxiliary effect on that path (vibrator, TTS, `startForeground` § 1016, the three sensor streams § 1017) — the tile was missed, not decided. Guarded inside `requestUpdate` so it is one door no future caller can walk around.
- [ ] **The `health` foreground-service type is unverified on hardware.** [§ 1016](../architecture/decisions.md) makes `startForegroundCompat` pass `location|health` on API 34+ when the platform's documented prerequisite holds, gated on `checkSelfPermission` and wrapped so a refusal retries with location alone. That answers the archived followup's caution that an unvalidated FGS-type edit can crash `startForeground`. What it does not answer is the thing the change is for: whether heart rate now genuinely survives the runner swiping back to the watch face. That needs a real watch and a run long enough to dim — the emulator synthesises HR and reproduces none of it. Pair it with the bench day the entry above wants.

## Surfaced by the #789 coverage round 30 — infra (2026-09-02)

Found reading `infra/` against its own comments and against the workflows that
consume it ([decisions §§ 889-893](../architecture/decisions.md)). Everything
fixable from source was fixed in that round; these three are what is left. The
first is an operator step on merged code, the second an owner call, the third a
sized-but-deliberately-unstarted asymmetry.

- [x] **Drop `kms:Decrypt` from the two GitHub deploy roles — the `terraform apply` it exists for is not something any workflow does.** **CLOSED 2026-09-02** ([decisions § 1021](../architecture/decisions.md)). Confirmed by measurement rather than by reading: `parseSteps` over all 21 workflows finds 59 jobs, exactly one credentialed (`release-web.yml:release`) and exactly one running `terraform` (`terraform.yml`, uncredentialed by design), and they are not the same job — the four `terraform apply` strings in `ci.yml` / `terraform.yml` are prose in their own comments. Both env roots now leave `kms_decrypt_principal_arn` at its `""` default and the now-unused `github_oidc` remote-state read went with it. **The premise the removal really rests on is one the filing did not state**: no `aws_lambda_function` sets `kms_key_arn`, so the deploy role's `lambda:GetFunction` / `UpdateFunctionCode` — which it does hold and the release does call eight times — never transits this key. All eight were read; none sets it. `scripts/check_infra_iam.mjs` claim 9 holds both premises in BOTH directions, so a wire restored while nothing exercises it fails as standing privilege and an empty wire once either premise breaks fails as a release that would `AccessDenied` mid-deploy. **Two module comments were false and are corrected**: the execution role does not "decrypt the sops env at cold-start" (`data.sops_file` decrypts at apply, the env vars are plaintext, and no `kms` reference exists anywhere under `apps/web/lambda/`), and the CMK does not encrypt the Lambda env vars. That leaves the EXECUTION role's own grant unexercised by the same argument — filed below rather than removed, because emptying the statement's identifiers leaves a principal-less statement KMS rejects. Original filing below. Both env stacks pass their OIDC deploy role in as `kms_decrypt_principal_arn`, putting it in the `AllowLambdaAndDeployRolesToDecrypt` statement of the env's secrets CMK — the key protecting `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`. `envs/prod/main.tf` justifies it as apply-time decryption "from the GitHub Actions runner"; **no workflow in this repo runs `terraform apply`.** `terraform.yml` runs `fmt` / `init -backend=false` / `validate` with no credentials by design, `release-web.yml` syncs S3 and updates eight Lambdas, `budgets.tf` states outright that these resources "are intended to be applied locally, not from CI", and `bin/deploy-prod.sh` applies under the operator's own SSO profile. The deploy policies carry no tfstate-bucket access and no `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration`, so the role could not finish an apply even with the decrypt. Not a path to plaintext on its own — the ciphertext lives in the private estate repo, which CI never checks out — but it is a grant the pipeline does not use on the one key in the account whose loss is unrecoverable. **Operator:** set `kms_decrypt_principal_arn = ""` in `infra/envs/prod/main.tf` and `infra/envs/preview/main.tf` (the module's `compact()` drops it from the statement's `identifiers`), then `terraform apply` in each env stack; the Lambda execution role is a separate identifier in the same statement and is untouched. Restore it the day a workflow genuinely applies. Not fixed in-round because it needs an apply and this lane holds no credentials. [decisions § 892](../architecture/decisions.md).
- [ ] **Owner call: should an Identity Center admin be able to decrypt production secrets?** Today one can, and it is deliberate — `AllowOperatorSopsUseViaIamPolicies` delegates Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey to the account root because `sops <file>`, `sops --set` (`bin/secret-set.sh`) and `sops updatekeys` (`bin/key-rotate.sh`) all decrypt before they re-encrypt, so an operator without Decrypt cannot rotate a secret at all. The key policy's own header claimed the opposite for as long as that statement had existed and is corrected in [decisions § 891](../architecture/decisions.md); what is left is the posture itself. Narrowing it means naming a dedicated operator principal in the key policy instead of root, which changes who holds the rotation flows and needs a decision about how that principal is assumed on a one-person estate — not a Terraform edit. Filed rather than done because the code change is the easy half and the wrong half to start with.
- [x] **`envs/preview` can set two of the three engine URLs; `envs/prod` can set all three.** **CLOSED 2026-09-02** ([decisions § 1024](../architecture/decisions.md)). Confirmed, and the "adding them before then is scaffolding" reading is wrong about what the change costs: the module input already exists and already defaults to `""`, so preview receives the same `""` before and after and the plan is byte-identical — the only thing that changes is that an operator CAN set it. Measured while confirming it, the asymmetry is **five** inputs wide, not one: `domain_name` (composed from `preview_subdomain`), the three reserved-concurrency caps (literals in preview WITH a stated reason), and `graph_cycle_url`, which was the only one with no reason recorded anywhere and the only one closed. `scripts/check_infra_coverage.mjs` claim 6 DERIVES the engine set from the module — a `_url` string input whose default is `""`, which is the value that means no engine and a graceful degrade — so a fourth engine is covered the day it lands with no registry to remember. Original filing below. `graph_cycle_url` is wired from a variable in `envs/prod/main.tf` and neither declared nor passed in `envs/preview/main.tf`, so preview takes the module default `""`, skips the graph-cycle generator and serves `round_trip`. Correct today and deliberate — preview has no sidecar to point at — but it is the only one of the three engine URLs preview cannot set, `graphhopper_url` and `osrm_url` are both declared there with exactly that "point it at an engine only if a preview must exercise the server-side path" rationale, and the asymmetry is recorded nowhere. Closing it is three lines (a variable, a wire, a description) the day a preview needs to exercise v3 loop generation; adding them before then is scaffolding for an engine that does not exist. [decisions § 893](../architecture/decisions.md).

## Surfaced by the #789 round 30 Lambda + edge-function coverage (2026-09-02)

Found while writing the coverage in [decisions §§ 894-898](../architecture/decisions.md). Each needs its own change rather than riding that round.

- [x] **The twenty in-app `PUBLIC_SITE_URL` folds under `src/routes/` still resolve the origin by hand.** Closed round 33 ([decisions § 970](../architecture/decisions.md)) — and the count was **twenty-two**, not twenty (the filing named six `/share/*` loaders where there are nine, and missed `sitemap.xml/+server.ts` and `u/[id]/+page.svelte`). The premise was also wrong: `||` catches the empty string but NOT a whitespace-only value, which is truthy and yielded a canonical of `   /share/run/<id>`. Original text: [§ 895](../architecture/decisions.md) routed the five production Lambdas through `siteOrigin` after finding they folded with `??`, which keeps an empty env var as the origin. The `src/` half spells it `env.PUBLIC_SITE_URL || DEFAULT_SITE_URL` in **twenty** places (`+page.ts` loaders for `/learn`, `/learn/[slug]`, `/learn/category/[category]`, `/recap/share/[id]`, six `/share/*` routes, plus the canonical `<svelte:head>` blocks on `/clubs/[slug]`, `/clubs/[slug]/events/[id]`, `/gym/[id]`, `/routes/[id]`, `/runs/[id]`, `/sessions/[id]`, and `/+page.ts`). `||` gets the blank case right, so none of them is wrong today — which is why this is filed rather than fixed in that round. What they do not do is trim a trailing slash, and none goes through the helper, so `siteOrigin` has five callers where it should have twenty-five and the rule lives in one place while twenty-five call sites re-decide it. The measurement is in the ADR: before § 895 the helper had **zero** callers, and its own doc comment states the rule the Lambdas were breaking. Closing this is a mechanical sweep plus widening `lambda_site_origin.test.ts`'s register to `src/routes/`.
- [x] **The coach Lambda dispatches its two sub-paths by substring, so the prod path table and the dev route table disagree about which paths exist.** Closed round 33 ([decisions § 967](../architecture/decisions.md)) — anchored dispatch, plus the half the filing missed: an unknown path under the prefix fell THROUGH to the coach turn under its 256 KB cap and now 404s. Original text: `rawPath.includes('/route-describe')` and `rawPath.includes('/route-request')`, against SvelteKit's exact `src/routes/api/coach/route-describe/+server.ts`. Measured: `POST /api/coach/x/route-describeZZ` reaches the route-describe handler and answers its `400 invalid route input`, where dev answers 404. Not exploitable — both sub-paths are Pro-gated and carry a **smaller** body cap (32 KB / 16 KB) than the coach path's 256 KB, so a mismatch routes a caller to a stricter handler, not a looser one. It becomes a defect the moment a third sub-path's name contains an existing one, at which point the first `includes` shadows it silently in production while dev routes both correctly. The fix is an anchored match on the path segment, and the case above belongs in `coach_lambda_handler.test.ts` beside the dispatch tests § 896 added.
- [x] **Five of the eight production Lambda handlers still have no behavioural test.** Already closed by PR #850 before round 33 opened; verified rather than fixed. All eight are imported and invoked: `coach` → `coach_lambda_handler.test.ts`, `generate-route` → `generate_lambda_handler.test.ts`, `osrm-proxy` → `osrm_proxy_lambda_handler.test.ts`, and all four share renderers plus `share-entity` → `share_lambda_handlers.test.ts`, which stubs `__SPA_SHELL_HTML__` and leaves the Supabase env unset so every lookup misses without a network call. The dispatch half the filing wanted reached IS reached — the two path regexes, the 404-vs-200 split and the 5-minute TTL are all asserted against a driven handler, not against source text. Original text: [§ 896](../architecture/decisions.md) covered `coach` and `generate-route`; `share-entity` already had one. `osrm-proxy` is importable with no native dependency and is the highest-value of the remainder — its request path IS the runner's waypoint coordinates, it is the only handler with a GET-only method gate, and its `allowDemoFallback: false` is what stops production leaking waypoints to the uncontracted `router.project-osrm.org` demo (issue #198), none of which is executed by anything. The four share/OG renderers (`share-run`, `share-route`, `share-badge`, `share-recap`) are harder and are why they were skipped: each imports an `@resvg` native `.node` addon and reads a build-time-substituted `__SPA_SHELL_HTML__`, so driving one needs either a stub for both or a split between the dispatch half and the render half. The dispatch half is the part worth reaching — the two path regexes, the 404-vs-200 split, and the 5-minute TTL on both, which today is asserted only as source text by `share_run_cache_control.test.ts`.
- [x] **The share Lambdas' catch-all 404 is the only response on those behaviours that sets no `cache-control`.** Closed round 33 ([decisions § 969](../architecture/decisions.md)) — and it was not the only one: the JSON **503** sets none either, and must NOT get the five-minute window (caching a transient failure at the edge turns a blip into a five-minute outage). Two headers, not one. Original text: Every other path in `share-run` / `share-route` / `share-badge` / `share-recap` / `share-entity` returns the deliberate `public, max-age=300, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60` ([decisions § 797](../architecture/decisions.md)'s privacy window); `jsonResponse(404, { error: 'not found' })` — the misconfiguration branch, reached when CloudFront sends a path the handler's regexes do not claim — sets only `content-type`, so the TTL is whatever the behaviour's cache policy decides rather than the five minutes the surface has chosen everywhere else. Low consequence (it is reachable only from a behaviour/dispatcher mismatch, which `share_entity_dispatch_guard.test.ts` already fails the PR for), but it is an inconsistency inside one file and the fix is one header.

## Surfaced by the #789 firmware round 30 (2026-09-02)

Found by the date comparison in [decisions § 899](../architecture/decisions.md):
for every `apps/custom_watch/core/src/<m>.rs` with a same-named
`apps/web/src/lib/**/<m>.ts`, compare `git log -1 --format=%cs` on each side.
**49 modules pair up; on 16 the web source moved after the port was last
touched.** Five of those were fixed this round ([§ 900](../architecture/decisions.md)
through [§ 903](../architecture/decisions.md)); the rest are below with the web
commit that moved them, so the next reader starts from a measurement rather than
from the sweep. Reported rather than half-fixed: each needs its own change, and
three of them need a decision about scope before any code.

- [x] **`fitness::RunSource` cannot represent `parkrun` or `race`, and has no cycling exclusion.** Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 996](../architecture/decisions.md). The source half was a real trap and is fixed: both variants added, and `is_qualifying` is now an exhaustive match rather than `!matches!(self, Other)`, so a variant added to the enum is a compile error until classified — web's stated reason for its total map, and the negated form was the same failure in the other direction. The **cycling exclusion is deliberately not ported** and `is_qualifying_run`'s doc says why: it needs an activity type `RunForFitness` has no producer for on a device with no sport selector, so the field would be unfillable and the case unreachable. The trigger that changes it is a phone push of run history, which would bring the field with its own wiring. Web `qualifyingRuns` gained `activity_type !== 'cycle'` in #747 and a total `Record<RunSource, boolean>` in #749, the latter to stop `parkrun` and `race` — a certified weekly 5K and a chip-timed official result, the two most authoritative sources there are — being silently omitted by an `||` chain. The watch's enum has seven variants ending in `Other`, and `is_qualifying` is `!matches!(self, Other)`, so both sources map to `Other` and are excluded, and there is no activity type on the wrist at all. Whether the watch should carry either is a scope question first: `qualifying_runs` has no consumer here (only `RecoveryAdvice` and `days_until_next_hard_session` are wired), and nothing pushes a per-run source over `SET1` today.
- [x] **`plan_progress` is missing `planWorkoutProgress`, added to web on 2026-08-11 (#757).** Closed 2026-09-02 as a recorded exclusion — [decisions § 997](../architecture/decisions.md). **The filing named one function; there are two** — `planDistanceBanked` is also absent and is part of the registered parity pair. Both need the plan's whole workout list and nothing pushes one: the two plan glance pages (`PlanReplan`, `PlanAdaptive`) render pre-computed views, and a per-week workout table has no wire and no room on a 168x96 panel. The two that ARE ported are ported because the phone sends their inputs. The exclusion and its trigger are now in the module doc rather than left as an unexplained count. Web's version excludes rest days from BOTH the numerator and the denominator, because the editor renders "Mark as done" on a rest day and a plan could therefore report over 100 % complete. Porting it is a new function rather than a repair, and there is no plan surface on the wrist, so this is a scope call.
- [x] **`streaks` has no `bestSince` bound, so a period card would report the all-time best.** Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 995](../architecture/decisions.md). Confirmed and worse than filed: **`recap.rs` carried its own private copy of the whole streak algorithm** and its own 512-day cap beside `streaks.rs`'s, so one crate held two implementations of one rule with only one registered as a parity port — a § 641 divergence that was undetectable by construction, and a bound added to one would have reached neither. The copy is gone, the bound is a REQUIRED parameter (a caller that forgets it is what produced this), and both the year and month builders pass one. Measured: twelve consecutive days in March 2024 gave a 2026 card a 12-day best and a `streak-7` badge, since `compute_recap_badges` grades off the same number. Web added the optional lower bound in #747 for exactly this: a 40-day streak from two years ago was the headline number on a card titled "My 2026 in running". `recap::build_year_in_running_recap` on the wrist calls the unbounded form, and `recap` is itself unwired — but the two move together, so port them together when either gets a surface.
- [x] **`roadbook` has no `RoadbookTarget` / `TARGET_BAND_FRACTION`.** Closed 2026-09-02 as a recorded exclusion plus a filed wire change — [decisions § 997](../architecture/decisions.md). **Both of the filing's premises are false.** `route_markers` carries `parse_cutoff` and no `parse_target`, so the input does not exist on the wrist; and `build_roadbook` has **no non-test caller** — the wired Roadbook glance renders the checkpoints the phone pushes over `RBK1`, so a field added to that function's output is one nothing on the device can read. The new box below carries the two-rail change. Web #768 (2026-08-15) added the per-checkpoint target-time verdict beside the cutoff one, graded on a PROPORTIONAL band because two minutes down at hour twenty of a 200-miler is noise where the same two minutes at a 30-minute checkpoint is not. The watch already carries `route_markers::parse_target`, so the input exists; the Roadbook glance page is wired, which makes this the one entry here with a real wrist surface waiting for it.
- [x] **`live_freshness` has neither `liveElapsedS` nor `raceClockS`.** Closed 2026-09-02 as a recorded exclusion — [decisions § 997](../architecture/decisions.md). Both reconstruct a clock a SPECTATOR cannot see; this device is the runner's own and `record::Recorder` owns the elapsed clock, so the distinction does not arise. The surface the filing worried about already makes it: `cutoff_eta::next_cutoff_eta` takes `elapsed_s`, the race clock, and `record.rs`'s `the_cutoff_eta_projects_from_race_pace_not_moving_pace` pins that it is not the moving one. Porting a reconstruction of a measured fact would give a second answer to a settled question. `freshness_for` stays ported because a ping's AGE does have a wrist analogue. Web added both after the port (#763 on 2026-08-13, #808 on 2026-08-24). The module doc correctly says only `freshnessFor` is ported, so the 5-against-16 test count is scope and not drift — but the race-clock distinction the two functions exist to draw (a ping's `elapsed_s` is the runner's recording timer, frozen at the last fix; a cut-off is measured against wall-clock time since the start) is one the wrist's own cut-off surfaces make, and it is worth a deliberate answer rather than an inherited silence.
- [x] **`recap`, `plan_replan`, `segments`, `auto_segment_effort`, `age_grade` each moved on web after the port and were read this round without a defect being found.** **CLOSED 2026-09-04** ([decisions § 1161](../architecture/decisions.md) + [§ 1162](../architecture/decisions.md) + [§ 1163](../architecture/decisions.md)). Measured this time rather than read: each web commit to the counterpart since the port's own commit was diffed, the Rust function read against it, and a discriminating input constructed where the two could answer differently. **Two of the five were divergent, and neither was the change the filing pointed at.** `recap.rs` filled a `Vec<i32, MAX_STREAK_DAYS>` with raw run days where the cap is named for distinct days, so 730 chronological runs across 2026 reported `{best: 256, current: 0}` against web's `{best: 365, current: 365}` — pre-existing, not #747, whose `bestSince` bound the firmware already had. `segments.rs` still carried `SegmentGenderFilter::Nonbinary` seven weeks after migration `20270422_001` deleted the value end-to-end — that IS #322, filed as comment-only because that is what it was in `age_grade.ts`; in `segments.ts` the same commit deleted a union member. Both fixed with pinning tests. The other three are identical for what the firmware ports, with the evidence stated in § 1163. Original filing: `recap` #747 bounds the streak (the entry above), `plan_replan` gained the generator-v2 P2 surface, `segments` #733 added a batched `computeEffortsFromTrack` plus an `unwrapLonDeg` bbox prefilter the watch has no analogue of, `auto_segment_effort` #733 is the call-site half of that batching, and `age_grade` #322 is a comment-only change. Recorded so a later sweep does not re-read them from zero — none is a known divergence, and none has been shown to be identical either.
- [x] **The wire format's altitude field cannot hold a Hardrock-class course.** Partly closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 994](../architecture/decisions.md) — and the widening itself refiled below as the two-rail change it is. Measured exactly, as asked: the ceiling is 3276.7 m (3276.75 m already stores `None`), `plausible_alt` admits to 9000 m, and **69 % of a Silverton-Handies-Silverton profile stores no elevation** — and because the gain rule carries the last reading across a dropout the summit push nets to **zero vert** rather than to a gap. **A second defect underneath it was fixed:** `ele_dm_from_m` accepted -3276.8 m and returned `Some(i16::MIN)`, which IS `ELE_NONE`, so the reading encoded to the sentinel and decoded back as `None` while the value one decimetre above stored fine — the function's doc asserted the opposite and its test pinned the wrong claim. Also recorded where a reader meets it: the bench checklist now says an empty ALT column over the high half of a mountain run is the format, not a dead barometer, and `the_altitude_ceiling_is_far_below_what_the_device_believes` pins the 69 % as characterisation. `run_store::TrackPoint::ele_dm` is an `i16` of decimetres, so `record_cadence::ele_dm_from_m` stores `None` above 3276.7 m — and `elevation::plausible_alt` admits up to 9000 m, so the whole band between them is a plausible reading the track cannot carry. Handies Peak (4,285 m) and Leadville's Hope Pass (3,840 m) are both inside it, which means a synced track from those races carries no elevation across exactly the section the vert is in. The code calls this out as a frozen limit that "tier-2 widens", so the decision is made; what was missing is a place where the consequence is written down in the runner's terms.

Found while mutation-testing the repo-level guard tier — see

that round did not own.

Original filing below. `tile_pack`, `streaks`, `fundraiser_progress`, `readiness`, `calories`, `column_limits`, `cycle_plan`, `text_limits` and `route_loop`. The version is not a guess: the last green CI run on `main` (5a81d206d) downloaded `deno-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.zip` from the **v2.9.6** release tag in both steps, so the pin reproduces exactly what CI ran green rather than proposing a version nothing has executed. The line stays COMMENTED in `.tool-versions`, like its `rust` / `golang` / `flutter` / `terraform` peers and unlike `nodejs` — the file's active lines are what `asdf install` materialises, and Deno is installed by its own installer here; the guard reads commented lines for exactly this reason. ## Surfaced by the #789 round 31 Edge Function coverage (2026-09-02)

Found reading the Deno tier against its own comments while writing
[decisions §§ 914-916](../architecture/decisions.md). The three defects those
entries record were fixed in-round; these four are what is left. Each needs a
change this lane could not make correctly — one crosses into a path the round
did not own, two are documented deliberate choices that deserve a second look
rather than a unilateral reversal, and one is a correctness question about a
third-party payload whose real shape is not knowable from here.

- [x] **`refresh-tokens` runs `verify_jwt = false` with no rate limit and no floor on `CRON_SECRET`, and its one sibling in that position has both.** The function's own header states the stake: without the gate "any attacker hitting it would loop the entire `integrations` table through Strava's OAuth refresh endpoint, burning Strava API quota and forcing token churn". Its only gate is `timingSafeEqual(token, cronSecret)` on a bearer the caller supplies. `strava-webhook` — same posture, same class of gate, reachable by URL alone — carries two defences this one does not: a 32-character minimum on its secret ("Defends against a misconfigured deploy (e.g. `STRAVA_WEBHOOK_SECRET=test`)") and a 60/hour IP-keyed bucket placed deliberately BEFORE the secret check, because "`timingSafeEqual` closes the per-byte channel but doesn't slow the offline guess rate". **The floor is the half that is unambiguously right and it could not land in this round**: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` sets `CRON_SECRET=ci-cron-secret` (15 characters) for the served-envelope lane, so adding the floor means editing a workflow this lane did not own, and a floor chosen to accommodate a CI fixture is not a floor. **The rate limit is the half that needs a decision, not a copy**: `ipBucketKey` collapses every caller the trusted header does not identify into one shared bucket, and it is not established that pg_cron's invocation carries `cf-connecting-ip`, so limiting before the compare could let an attacker starve the hourly token refresh out of the same bucket. Spending the bucket only on a FAILED compare bounds the guess rate without that risk, and is a deliberate divergence from the sibling rather than an oversight — which is the call to make. **The floor half was closed 2026-09-02 at round-31 integration** — [decisions § 937](../architecture/decisions.md): the floor is in, the CI fixture was lengthened to clear it rather than the floor lowered to fit the fixture, and a source guard now reads both plus the sibling's. **The rate-limit half closed 2026-09-02 in round 33** — [decisions § 973](../architecture/decisions.md): the call the filing framed correctly, made the way it framed it. The bucket is spent on a failed compare rather than in front of it, so pg_cron cannot be starved out of the shared `unknown` bucket and the authorised path acquires no database dependency; it is narrowed once more to a bearer that was actually SUPPLIED, because a bearerless POST is a probe rather than a guess — which also keeps the sibling's 60/hour ceiling honest against a CI lane that would otherwise have spent 62 of it. `gate_invariants.test.ts` pins both placements, this function's and the sibling's opposite one.
- [x] **`strava-import`'s `sync` action is the only rate limit in the file that fails open, and it is the expensive one.** `connect` and `disconnect` both pass `{ failClosed: true }`; `sync` does not, on the stated grounds that it is "idempotent and read-mostly". The resource it spends is not ours: a sync walks up to ~20 pages of Strava's API and uploads a track per activity, against Strava's **per-application** budget. So on an RPC blip the guard disappears from the one action whose cost lands on a shared third-party quota, while the two cheap single-write actions stay guarded — the posture is inverted relative to `_shared/rate_limit.ts`'s own rule ("expensive paths where letting traffic through on RPC failure is worse than the false-positive denial"). The same open posture is on `parkrun-import` (an outbound scrape of parkrun.org.uk on our IP, whose own comment names IP-reputation drain as the threat), `race-results-import` and `race-listings-sync` (outbound calls carrying **our** RunSignUp / ChronoTrack / UltraSignup credentials). Left as filed rather than flipped because a false 503 during a DB blip is a user-visible regression on four live paths and the rationale on the `sync` leg is written down, not accidental. **Closed 2026-09-02 in round 33** — [decisions § 974](../architecture/decisions.md). All four flipped, and the reason the filing's own hesitation dissolves is that the fail-open rescues nothing: the RPC that failed is `check_rate_limit` against the SAME database each of these four must then write its rows to, so the request was going to fail anyway and the only variable is whether it burns a third party's budget first. The count was as filed — 13 call sites, 9 already fail-closed, and the 4 open ones exactly the 4 spending a resource that is not ours. `_shared/rate_limit_failclosed_guard.test.ts` now reads every call site in the tree by paren-balanced argument extraction and requires the posture on each.
- [x] **The UltraSignup leg reads one athlete's WHOLE history and stamps every result with a single listing's name, date and distance.** `ultraSignUpResultsUrl` hits `/service/events.svc/results/athlete?uid=…` — an athlete feed, not a race feed — and there is no race parameter on it. Every row it returns is then mapped through `mapOpts`, which carries the ONE `public_race_listings` row the request named, so a runner with twenty past ultras gets twenty `runs` rows all dated on the target race's date, all at the target race's distance, all pointing at its `race_listing_id`; their `external_id`s differ only by bib. `ultraSignUpScopeGate` does not cover this — it only requires an athlete id, which is what makes the feed athlete-scoped in the first place. Today the hole is closed by the absence of data rather than by a check (nothing populates UltraSignup listings; the listing sync is a stub), and the leg is credential-gated, so it is inert. **Note that [decisions § 914](../architecture/decisions.md) slightly widens the reachable path**: before it, two of those historical races sharing a bib raised 23505 and lost the whole batch, which accidentally blocked some of this; now the batch is deduped and inserts. The fix needs a field to attribute a result to the race with, and `UltraSignUpResult` declares none — closing it means either reading UltraSignup's real payload for a race identifier and filtering on it, or refusing the leg outright until one exists. Guessing at a field name from here would be worse than filing it. **Closed 2026-09-02 in round 33 by refusing** — [decisions § 975](../architecture/decisions.md). The filing was right in every particular and the harm was measured: three results from three different races become three `runs` rows differing only in bib and finishing time, all at the target race's date and distance. `ultraSignUpAttributionGate()` refuses at both doors — the import branch (before the credential read and before the fetch) and the availability probe, which previously answered on key presence and so would have advertised the tile the moment the key landed. The code is `503 provider_not_configured` because that is the seam both clients already disable their tile on, with `reason: 'results_unattributable'` so an operator who HAS set the key is not sent hunting. The mapper, extractor and URL builder stay standing behind the gate; the gate's doc says lifting it costs an OBSERVED payload plus a filter on the race id, not just deleting the gate.
- [x] **`parkrun-import` truncates silently at `MAX_PARKRUN_ROWS` and the response cannot say so.** The scrape loop stops at 5000 rows and answers `{ imported, skipped }`, where `skipped` means "already had it" — there is no `truncated` or `complete` field, so a caller cannot distinguish a whole import from a capped one. This is the shape the repo already litigates on the Strava side, where `parseStravaSyncResult` treats an absent `complete` as PARTIAL on purpose. Filed rather than fixed because it is not reachable in practice: 5000 parkruns is roughly 96 years of weekly Saturdays, and the most prolific parkrunner alive is around a fifth of the way there. It becomes worth the field the day the cap is lowered or a second table on the page starts contributing rows. **Closed 2026-09-02 in round 33** — [decisions § 976](../architecture/decisions.md) — and the reachability estimate held, which is why the fix went wider than the box. parkrun now answers `{ imported, skipped, total, complete }`, the walk counting past the cap instead of stopping dead at it (the same statement bounded the result set and destroyed the evidence that it had been bounded). **The same class one function over is reachable today**: `race-results-import`'s three extractors cap at `MAX_RESULTS_ROWS` (2000) and `runSignUpResultsUrl` narrows upstream by USER ID only, so a bib-scoped request fetches the whole finisher field and the bib filter runs afterwards — driven at 30,000 finishers, the caller's bib 25000 is not in the extracted 2,000 and they are told no result was found for a race they finished. That leg now reports `complete` on every success shape and answers `502 upstream_results_truncated` when a truncated fetch matched nothing. Default is `parseStravaSyncResult`'s (absent = PARTIAL), not `cloudExportShortfall`'s, for the stated reason: one transport, shipped with its callers.
## Surfaced by the #789 coverage round 31 — web unit lane (2026-09-02)

Found reading the 156 `apps/web/src/lib/` files #789 touched against their own
stated contracts ([decisions §§ 919-923](../architecture/decisions.md)).
Everything the lane could close without editing a Dart file was closed in that
round; these are what is left. The first two are halves of a parity pair, which
this round could not touch on one side only.

- [x] **`OffRouteAlertDetector` treats an unusable distance reading as "off route", so a non-finite value arms a safety escalation rather than suppressing it.** `update(offRouteDistanceMetres, nowMs)` documents `null` as "on-route / no route selected / no GPS fix" and resets the clock on it, but the guard is `offRouteDistanceMetres == null || offRouteDistanceMetres <= this.thresholdM` — and `NaN <= 75` is `false`, as is `Infinity <= 75`. So a reading the geometry could not produce starts the 90-second sustain clock and, if it persists, fires the once-per-run escalation to the runner's trusted contacts off a measurement nobody has. It also latches, so the false fire consumes the real one. The reachable path is `run_recorder`'s `_offRouteDistance`, which seeds `minDist = double.infinity` and returns it unchanged if every `d < minDist` comparison is false — which is what a route carrying a non-finite waypoint produces. Low probability, high consequence, and the fix is one line on each side: treat a non-finite distance exactly as `null`. **Not fixed in-round because this is a TS↔Dart parity pair (`off_route_alert`) and the two sides are byte-for-byte equivalent today; fixing web alone would create the divergence the pair exists to prevent.** The same edit is owed to `apps/mobile_android/lib/off_route_alert.dart`, where the only surface actually lives.
- [x] **The same detector wedges permanently if the device clock steps backwards while the runner is off route.** `sinceMs` is stamped from `nowMs` on the first off-route snapshot and never re-examined, so an NTP correction that moves the clock back makes `nowMs - this.sinceMs` negative for the rest of that off-route stretch and the alert can never fire. It self-heals only if the runner returns on-route (which resets `sinceMs`) and leaves again — i.e. it fails exactly in the case where they do not come back. `recentRunVolume` and `comebackLoad` both already clamp a future-stamped sample for the mirror-image reason, so the codebase has the idiom; this detector does not use it. Same parity-pair constraint as the entry above, and the same one-line shape: clamp `sinceMs` down to `nowMs` when the clock has moved behind it.
- [x] **`normaliseE164` claims to fold "the hyphen family" and folds three of its seven members.** `SEPARATORS` carries `-` (U+002D), U+2011 and U+2013, and omits U+2010 HYPHEN, U+2012 FIGURE DASH, U+2014 EM DASH and U+2212 MINUS SIGN — all of which a contact card, a CRM export or a word processor's autocorrect will put inside a pasted phone number. The failure is in the safe direction (the number is refused, not silently altered into a different reachable one, which is the case the `(0)` repair exists for) so nothing misdelivers; what it costs is an owner being told a correct number is invalid with no hint as to which character did it. Parity pair `e164`, identical on both sides today, so the class has to widen on both at once.
- [x] **`classifyStravaRow` imports a row of unknown activity type as a run, and the header index has no way to say the column is missing.** An empty `Activity Type` cell falls through the `t && !t.includes(...)` guard to `import`, and `importOne` then defaults `actType` to `'run'`. That is correct for a blank cell in a normal export, but `indexHeader` returns `-1` for a header it cannot find and `row[-1]` is `undefined`, so a Strava export era that renames the column would import a migrant's entire history — rides, swims, yoga — as runs, silently, with the disposition counter reporting them as imported. The required-column check covers only `Activity ID` and `Filename`. Worth deciding whether a missing type column is a fatal header error (matching the other two) or whether the unknown-type row should be dropped as `unsupported`; either is a behaviour change, which is why it is filed rather than taken. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 979](../architecture/decisions.md): a header naming NO activity type is refused alongside the other two required columns (with the column absent, every row is untyped, so dropping them all reports zero imported and several thousand dropped — a worse message than a named header failure), and `type` now falls back to `Sport Type` so an era that renames only the coarse column still imports. The blank CELL keeps its lenient `run` default deliberately. Web-only: the mobile importer does not share the shape.
- [x] **`cloudExportJobFromResponse` casts `format` where it grades everything else.** The function's own doc block is about being fail-closed in two directions and it is, for `status` and for a `ready` job with no URL — but `format: str(body.format) as CloudExportFormat | undefined` takes whatever string the server sent. A server answering `format: "zip"` renders "zip" on the export card. Cosmetic only (nothing branches on it) which is why it is not in the round, but it is the one unvalidated field in a module whose contract is that there are none. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 980](../architecture/decisions.md). The "renders 'zip' on the export card" premise was wrong: neither client renders the field, web reads it only as `=== 'gpx'` / `=== 'backup'` and mobile only as `== 'csv'`. What was real is that the cast made the TYPE a claim the value had never been checked against. Graded on both rails of the `cloud_export_helpers` parity pair at once — the Dart half took the same raw string — and mirrored to the iOS twin.
## Surfaced by the #789 native round 31 (2026-09-02)

- [x] **Neither Go service runs `go test -race` in CI, so the concurrency in the live hub is never exercised by the detector.** `ci.yml`'s `Test job_worker (Go)` and `Test graph_cycle sidecar (Go)` jobs both run a plain `go test ./...`. The job_worker binary is the most concurrent thing in the repo — an in-process pub/sub hub with per-room goroutines, a GC sweeper, a bridge poller, an atomic heartbeat and six HTTP servers on one mux — and nothing has ever run the race detector over it in CI. Both suites are race-clean today, measured locally on `test/789-r31-native`: `job_worker` 20 s → 35 s and `graph_cycle` 5 s → 5.5 s with `-race`, so the cost is one job-minute. Not fixed in-round because `.github/workflows/ci.yml` belongs to no lane this round; the change is `-race` on those two `go test` lines and nothing else (both jobs are already in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:`). Closed 2026-09-02 at round-31 integration — [decisions § 935](../architecture/decisions.md).
- [x] **The app has two elevation-gain rules and reports different vert for the same track depending on which surface asks.** `runs/run_stats.ts` `elevationGainMetres` sums every upward delta with no noise gate; `routes/route_simplify.ts` `computeElevationGain` gates at `ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M` (3 m) and resets the reference on a real descent. Both carry the dropout carry-forward, so the difference is purely the gate. A run shown as climbing N metres therefore becomes a route claiming materially less the moment the runner taps "save as route", with no explanation anywhere — and on a barometer-noisy or GPS-altitude track the gap is large, which is the case the gate exists for. Both watch ports now match their own source ([decisions § 902](../architecture/decisions.md) for the run-stats one, [§ 925](../architecture/decisions.md) for the route one), so the rails are faithful and the inconsistency is upstream of them, on web, where it is a product decision rather than a port question: either the run stat should gate too, or the two should be documented as answering different questions. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 981](../architecture/decisions.md): the run stat now delegates to `computeElevationGain`, so there is one rule. It was not a product decision after all — **mobile has never had the second rule** (`run_detail_screen.dart` reads a run's climb through the Dart `computeElevationGain`), so the same run was reading differently on web and on the phone and documenting the split would have been writing down a bug. Measured on an AR(1) altitude-error model before deciding: a flat 30-minute run with barometer-grade error reported 143 m of climb ungated against 3 m gated, a real 200 m climb 267 m against 197 m, and a clean noise-free track 225 m on both.
- [x] **`route_geometry`'s `markerPointAtDistance` has no watch port, and the omission is not written down anywhere.** **CLOSED — already done, verified 2026-09-02.** The module doc of `apps/custom_watch/core/src/route_geometry.rs` has named the exclusion since `69839feca` (#848): "Web additionally carries `markerPointAtDistance`, the marker-authoring inverse; it has no wrist surface and is not ported, which is why the suites are 36 here against web's 43 rather than equal." Counts re-measured: 43 `test(` blocks in the web suite, 36 `#[test]` in the Rust one, and exactly 7 of the web blocks are `markerPointAtDistance` cases — 43 − 7 = 36, so the gap is entirely and only this. (An eighth web block mentions the function incidentally inside a `distanceAlongRoute` case, which is why a naive grep says 8.) Original filing below. Seven of the web module's 43 cases are that function; the other 36 are mirrored one-for-one, so the count gap is entirely this. It is the route-editor "place this course marker at mile 5" path and authoring is web-canonical per [§ 24](../architecture/decisions.md#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive), so leaving it out is almost certainly right — but the module doc claims the port without naming the exclusion, which is how a later reader reads a 36-vs-43 count as drift. Either state the exclusion in the module doc or port it; do not leave the count unexplained.
- [x] **`unfed::Unfed::ALL` and `UnfedClass::ALL` are hand-written registers that a new variant can silently miss, and the width assertions iterate them.** **CLOSED — verified 2026-09-02.** Closed by [decisions § 960](../architecture/decisions.md) in `9bb122d64` (#851); the box was never ticked. Re-verified independently on this round's base: `apps/custom_watch/core/src/unfed.rs` now carries a `#[cfg(test)]` module that reads its own source with `include_str!` and holds both `ALL` arrays against the enum bodies they claim to enumerate (`every_unfed_variant_is_registered_in_all`, `every_unfed_class_variant_is_registered_in_all`), plus the two distinctness checks the filing asked for (`no_two_reasons_read_the_same`, `no_two_classes_share_a_slot_token`) and the hint-class pairing. Both parsers carry a floor on the variant count and an is-identifier check, so a body this parse cannot speak for fails loudly rather than reporting agreement over zero variants. The module went from zero runtime tests to five. Original filing below. `class()` and `reason()` are exhaustive matches, so adding a variant forces both to be updated — but `ALL` is a plain array, and the `const` block that asserts every reason fits `face::COLS` walks it. A variant added without registering therefore compiles with a reason of any width and draws off the panel, on the one module whose entire purpose is that every empty page speaks one vocabulary. Nothing checks that two variants do not share a `reason()` string either, which would defeat the same purpose from the other direction. The module has zero runtime tests today (its coverage is the `const` block alone). A source-level guard counting enum variants against the array, plus a distinctness check over `reason()` and `slot_token()`, is the shape.
- [x] **`ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M` now exists on three rails and is registered in none of them, which is exactly how it came to be missing from one.** Web `routes/route_simplify.ts` `ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M = 3`, mobile `route_simplify.dart` `kElevationGainMinDeltaM`, and — since [decisions § 925](../architecture/decisions.md) — `watch_core::route_simplify::ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M`. `scripts/check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs`'s `CONSTANT_ROWS` is the registry built for exactly this shape (it already holds the off-route hysteresis and five Minetti constants across four rails each, with `rustConst` / `dartConst` / `tsConst` readers), and one row would make a future one-sided change fail the `watch-wire-vectors` job instead of shipping. Not added in-round because `scripts/` belongs to no lane this round; the entry is `rustRail(RS_ROUTE_SIMPLIFY, rustConst('ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M'))`, `dartRail('apps/mobile_android/lib/route_simplify.dart', dartConst('kElevationGainMinDeltaM'))`, `otherRail('apps/web/src/lib/routes/route_simplify.ts', tsConst('ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M'))` — a `why` naming the noise gate, and nothing else. The same argument applies to the 5 m span in `isTrackRenderable`, which is a bare literal on all three rails. Row added 2026-09-02 at round-31 integration and mutation-checked on each of the three rails — [decisions § 936](../architecture/decisions.md); the `isTrackRenderable` span is still open, and needs naming on each rail first.
- [x] **`training_load::median` panics on an empty slice, and its only caller's emptiness guard is the whole proof.** **CLOSED — verified 2026-09-02.** Closed by [decisions § 961](../architecture/decisions.md) in `9bb122d64` (#851); the box was never ticked. Re-verified: the signature is `fn median(xs: &mut [f64]) -> Option<f64>` and it returns `None` on an empty slice before the `xs[mid - 1]` that used to underflow, `compute_calibration` folds the emptiness branch into the same expression, and `median_of_nothing_is_none_rather_than_a_panic` pins it. Original filing below. `xs.len() / 2` is 0 for an empty slice, `0.is_multiple_of(2)` is true, and `xs[mid - 1]` then underflows — in release, where `overflow-checks = false`, that wraps to `usize::MAX` and the index panics anyway. `compute_calibration` returns early on `trimps_per_km.is_empty()` so it is unreachable today, and the NaN half of the same function was closed this round ([decisions § 926](../architecture/decisions.md)).
