## Surfaced by the #789 round 33 mobile lane (2026-09-02)

Seven items were closed in-round with their pinning tests
([decisions §§ 985-991](../architecture/decisions.md)), including the
`sync_service_test.dart` flake that had `main` red. What follows is what this
lane found and could not take.

- [x] **Moving `ActivityType` out of `preferences.dart` needs an edit to `apps/web/scripts/check_constraint_unions.mjs`, which no mobile lane may make.** The filed item is exactly right — `csv_run_importer.dart`, a pure parser, imports `preferences.dart show ActivityType`, and `preferences.dart` imports `package:flutter/material.dart` because the enum carries an `IconData get icon`. Verified this round: the enum is referenced from **31** files under `apps/mobile_android/lib`, and `packages/core_models` has no Flutter dependency at all (only `flutter_lints`, a dev dep), so the `icon` getter cannot travel with it and must become an extension in a Flutter-side file — `activity_type_labels.dart` is the natural host, since it already resolves the label the enum deliberately does not carry. **The blocker is one registry line.** `check_constraint_unions.mjs` registers the rail as `{ file: 'apps/mobile_android/lib/preferences.dart', decl: 'ActivityType', shape: 'enum' }` for `runs.activity_type`; the guard parses the enum out of that exact file, so moving the declaration fails the `parity-types` job until that path changes to the new home. A re-export does not satisfy a `shape: 'enum'` rail. Web already has the shape this should copy — a leaf `apps/web/src/lib/runs/activity_type.ts` holding `ACTIVITY_TYPES` beside the `types.ts` union — so the durable mobile answer is a leaf `packages/core_models/lib/src/activity_type.dart`. Do it in a change that owns both trees, or hand the one-line registry edit to whoever owns `apps/web/scripts/`. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1013](../architecture/decisions.md). The round-34 mobile lane owned both trees, so the declaration and both registry lines moved together. `IconData get icon` became an extension in `activity_type_labels.dart`; `splitIntervalMetresFor` could not travel either, for the opposite reason (it reads `DistanceUnit`, still in `preferences.dart`), and is an extension there.
- [x] **28 mobile test files pair a temp directory with widget taps and no `pumpUntil` at all.** Measured while closing [§ 991](../architecture/decisions.md): 86 files under `apps/mobile_android/test/` create a temp directory, 51 delete it in a `tearDown` and 29 in an `addTearDown`, and 28 of them drive the UI (`tester.tap` / `pumpAndSettle`) without ever waiting on a store's own completion signal — `dashboard_screen_test`, `home_screen_test`, `run_screen_test`, `runs_screen_test`, `settings_screen_test`, `you_screen_test` and 22 more. That is the population of the § 723 residue class, not its membership: `pumpAndSettle` is the right wait for a purely-visual assertion, and only a test whose tap starts real store I/O it then fails to wait for is an actual member. Separating the two needs the whole suite run with `pumpUntil` (and the store's `notifyListeners`) instrumented to log ordering, which is a full-sweep run this lane's environment caps forbid. The technique is written down in § 723 and § 990 and worked both times it was used; the run is the missing part. Partly closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1012](../architecture/decisions.md). Rather than auditing the 28, the § 991 SHAPE was searched for in the production code and found in exactly two places, both in `LocalRunStore`'s in-progress recording path — the one path deliberately kept off the serialised write chain, so `debugWritesSettled()` never answered for it, and both of whose drivers discard the future. It now has its own `debugInProgressSettled()`. The two named members wait on it. The remaining population stands as § 991 left it, but the two ROOT CAUSES are gone.
- [x] **A permanent per-run upload failure other than a non-finite waypoint would still retry forever.** [§ 986](../architecture/decisions.md) removed the one such failure that was known, and deliberately did not build a terminal-error taxonomy for a category that would then have no member. The candidate that remains unmeasured is a track blob past the `runs` bucket's object-size limit: `saveRunsBatch` catches it per-run, leaves the run unsynced, and the next cycle re-gzips the same bytes and fails identically. Measuring it needs the bucket's configured limit and a synthetic ultra-length track; if such a class exists, the answer is a classifiable terminal failure the drain parks plus a surface that tells the runner, not a retry cap. Measured 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1009](../architecture/decisions.md). **It is reachable**, and the category now has a member. A track blob gzips to 27.3 bytes per waypoint (flat from 3.6k to 500k points), so the bucket's 25 MiB limit is 959,883 waypoints: 266.6 hours of 1 Hz recording, which the recorder cannot reach, but a 94.3 MiB GPX that deflates to 8.3 MiB — sixty times inside the 500 MiB cap `importFromZip` puts on a Strava archive. Closed at the source (the uploader refuses an over-size blob before spending the network, with a typed `TrackTooLargeException` that `classifyImportFailure` buckets as `tooLarge`). The PARK half is filed below rather than half-built.
- [x] **`RunRow.toJson` can still hand `jsonEncode` a value it refuses.** [§ 986](../architecture/decisions.md) made the DOMAIN `Run.toJson` total, which covers the local store and the backup archive. The generated `RunRow` is a separate serializer on the PostgREST path: `runRowFromRun` screens every double it lifts out of the metadata bag through `runPromotedDouble`'s finiteness check but passes `run.distanceMetres` straight through, and the `upsert` body is JSON-encoded by the supabase client. That specific hole is closed at the source (the domain object cannot carry a non-finite distance past `toJson` any more, and `runs_distance_m_check` refuses one server-side since § 939), so this is a latent shape rather than a live defect — a future writer that builds a `RunRow` directly rather than through a `Run` would reopen it. The durable close is for the generated `toJson` to emit only encodable values, which is a `gen_dart_models.dart` change of the same shape as § 985's. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1010](../architecture/decisions.md). The filing called it "a latent shape rather than a live defect"; measured, it is **live, and four holes rather than one**. § 986 screened the domain serializer's OUTPUT while `runRowFromRun` reads the FIELDS, and the object a sync drain uploads is the resident one, not the screened copy written to disk. Fixed in `runRowFromRun` rather than in `gen_dart_models.dart`: what a non-finite value MEANS is a per-column question, so `distance_m` coerces to 0 through a shared `storableDistanceMetres` and a bag key is dropped.
- [x] **KMZ route import needs a bytes pipeline, not just a parser.** [§ 988](../architecture/decisions.md) widened mobile route import to GPX / KML / GeoJSON / TCX and removed every promise of KMZ rather than adding it. The parser side is nearly free: `archive` is **already a transitive dependency** of this workspace (`pubspec.lock`), it is pure Dart, and `RouteParser.fromKmz` would be a `ZipDecoder` call handing the inner document to the existing `fromKml`. The cost is the pipeline: `routes_screen._pickAndImport` and `SharedFileImportService.importPath` both `File.readAsString()`, and both hand a `String` through a `compute` isolate request to `routeFromImportedFile` — and `readAsString` throws on a zip before any parser is reached. Widening means those two reads become `readAsBytes`, the two isolate request types carry bytes, and the dispatch decodes to text per format. Web has done this since it was written (JSZip), so this is a real parity gap, not a design difference.

## Surfaced by the #789 round 33 Edge Function lane (2026-09-02)

Six items were taken in-round ([decisions §§ 973-977](../architecture/decisions.md)).
What follows is what this lane found and could not take, either because the
artefact lives in `apps/web/` or `apps/mobile_*` (which no lane owned this
round) or because the change is a product decision rather than a defect fix. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1025](../architecture/decisions.md). § 988's honesty was verified first and holds. Built: both entry points read bytes, the two isolate requests carry them, and `routeTextFromImportedBytes` unwraps a KMZ before the unchanged string-typed dispatch. `archive` needed no new dependency and `gpx_parser` stays dependency-free.
- [x] **`isProviderConfigured` fails open on the phone, and the filing's "same question on web" is false — web is already fail-closed and is the reference implementation.** Counted, as the box asks: there is **ONE** logical copy of the fail-open shape, in `apps/mobile_android/lib/race_service.dart` plus its iOS twin. Web has **none**: all three probes (`isRunSignUpConfigured` / `isUltraSignUpConfigured` / `isChronoTrackConfigured`) route through `isProviderNotConfigured`, which returns "not configured" for a 429, any 5xx, an unreadable cross-origin body and a status-0 `FunctionsFetchError`, each with a comment naming the missing-credential rule. Only a readable non-429 4xx reads as configured there. The Dart twin answers `true` for every one of those cases (`on FunctionException catch (e) { … return true; }` plus a bare `catch (_) { return true; }`), so **the two platforms disagree about a configured provider whenever the probe does not cleanly reach the gate** — and the filing's other observation is confirmed: `races_screen.dart`'s `_probe()` wraps the call in a try/catch that can never fire, because `isProviderConfigured` swallows everything. Fix is to port web's grading to Dart (429 and 5xx and a transport failure all read as unavailable), mirror to the iOS twin, and then the screen-level catch becomes reachable and can go. Not taken here: `apps/mobile_*` is outside this lane. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1007](../architecture/decisions.md). Web's grading is ported to `raceProbeUnavailable`, a top-level pure function so the decision is testable without a client. One correction: the dead `_probe()` catch was NOT removed. It is unreachable, but web's own callers of these probes carry the identical `try { … } catch { available = false }`, the sibling `_run()` in the same file wraps the equally-total `searchRaceListings`, and a probe is the layering contract's named example of an auxiliary network effect — deleting it on the phone alone would create a divergence in the file the change exists to close.
- [x] **Both clients probe the wrong function for the UltraSignup RESULTS tile, and after [§ 975](../architecture/decisions.md) that is now materially wrong.** Web's `isUltraSignUpConfigured` and mobile's `raceImportProviders['ultrasignup'].probeFunction` both invoke `race-listings-sync` with `{ provider: 'ultrasignup' }`. That answers for the **listings sync** leg, which is real and legitimately gated on `ULTRASIGNUP_API_KEY`. The **results-import** leg now refuses unconditionally (the athlete feed carries no race identifier), so provisioning the key would light up an import tile whose very next call 503s. The two happened to agree while both gated on the same env vars; they no longer do. Fix is one line per platform: probe `race-results-import` with `{ provider: 'ultrasignup', probe: true }`, exactly as the ChronoTrack spec already does. `race-listings-sync` must NOT be made to lie about its own leg to paper over this. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1008](../architecture/decisions.md). Verified against both clients and both functions before applying; the one-line fix per platform was right. The guard on each platform derives its premise (it reads the probe branch and asserts UltraSignup is still refused independently of its credential) rather than restating the fix, so lifting § 975 tells the next reader to re-decide instead of deleting an assertion. **RunSignUp was deliberately left probing the sync** — see the round-34 filing below.
- [x] **Nothing reads the `complete` flag either importer now returns.** `parkrun-import` answers `{ imported, skipped, total, complete }` and `race-results-import` answers `complete` on every success shape ([§ 976](../architecture/decisions.md)), and the contract is `parseStravaSyncResult`'s — **an absent `complete` is PARTIAL**. Today the field is honest and unread on both platforms, so a capped parkrun import and a 2,000-finisher-truncated race import still present as whole. The web Strava side already has the parser and the copy to mirror (`strava_sync_result.ts` ↔ `strava_sync_result.dart` + the shortfall banner); this wants the same shape for the two scrapers, plus a sentence for the new `502 upstream_results_truncated`, which today falls through to a generic import-failed message on both clients. Closed 2026-09-02 — [decisions § 1014](../architecture/decisions.md). `parseImportCompleteness` grades both, fail-closed in `parseStravaSyncResult`'s direction and for that rule's own reason (one transport per importer, shipped alongside its callers). Three shared `integrations.*` keys across seven web catalogues and seven ARBs, all phrased to avoid grammatical-number agreement because the noun in the "n of total" sentence agrees with the TOTAL, not the count. The 502 `upstream_results_truncated` has its own sentence on both platforms.
- [ ] **Lifting the UltraSignup refusal needs a payload, not a code change.** [§ 975](../architecture/decisions.md)'s gate is deliberately not liftable on its own: `ultraSignUpAttributionGate()` refuses because `UltraSignUpResult` declares no field naming which race a row came from, and deleting the gate restores the mis-attribution exactly. Closing it is (1) observe UltraSignup's real `/service/events.svc/results/athlete?uid=` response and record the race identifier's field name, (2) add it to the row shape and filter mapped rows against the listing's `provider_race_id`, (3) then remove the gate — in that order, in one change. `ultrasignup_attribution.test.ts`'s first case is a characterisation test that goes red the day the mapper CAN attribute, which is the signal to do this.
- [ ] **`race-listings-sync`'s field names and endpoints are unverified against a live payload.** [§ 977](../architecture/decisions.md) writes the whole path behind the unchanged credential gate and handles the unverifiable half explicitly — every reading is optional-with-drop and counted, so a differently-shaped feed answers `synced: 0` with `unusable` equal to the row count on the first call, and a wrong endpoint answers a non-2xx which is refused `502`. What is still owed the day a key arrives: one real call, then reconcile `readRunSignUpRace` / `readUltraSignUpRace` / `providerRacesUrl` / `extractProviderRaces` against what came back. Two specific things to check first — whether `distance_units` really spells miles `M` (the unit table refuses both `M` and `m` on purpose, since folding them files a 100-mile race as a 100-metre one), and whether the date is month-first (a day-first feed announces itself on the first race past the 12th of a month, and everything before that is silently transposed).
- [ ] **Nothing ever calls `race-listings-sync` with `sync: true`.** The sync is opt-in ([§ 977](../architecture/decisions.md)) because every existing caller is a credential probe and a page load must not walk a provider feed. That means the calendar still fills from nothing until something asks: a `pg_cron` schedule (the `refresh-tokens` shape, with its own `CRON_SECRET` gate — note this function is `verify_jwt = true` today, so a cron caller needs a different door), or an operator-triggered admin surface, or a "refresh races near me" affordance on `/races` sized to the 2/hour bucket. That is a product decision, not a defect, and it is the last step of #10.

## Surfaced by the #789 round 34 — web lane (2026-09-02)

- [x] **One JS comment stripper is still hand-rolled, and it is a register entry away from being the tenth.** [§ 1000](../architecture/decisions.md) single-sourced eleven copies into `core/strip_comments.ts` and left exactly one: `src/lib/integrations/strava_zip_strictness.test.ts` spells the two-`replace` variant, because `src/lib/integrations` belonged to another lane in that round. It is not merely duplication — that variant is one of the two that never handled a `/*` inside a string literal, and the module it scans (`strava-zip.ts`) is a parser full of quoted path fragments. The change is four lines: delete the local `stripComments`, import the shared one, delete its entry from the `REGISTER` in `security_guards.test.ts`. The guard fails the moment the entry goes stale, so the two halves cannot be done separately. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1033](../architecture/decisions.md). The box's own question was answered first and the answer was no: `strava-zip.ts` spells no block-comment delimiter anywhere, in code or in a string, so the two strippers were measured byte-identical on it. A latent hole, closed with its register entry in the same commit.
- [x] **The single-source guard keys on the BLOCK strip, so a JS scanner that blanks only `//` would still slip through.** [§ 1000](../architecture/decisions.md)'s register detects a hand-rolled stripper by the `/\*[\s\S]*?\*\/` needle, which every one of the eleven copies happened to spell. A new guard that blanks line comments alone would be wrong — the prose above a rule frequently sits in a `/** … */` block — and nothing would say so. It was not closed in-round because the line-strip spellings do not enumerate cleanly (`/^\s*\/\//`, `/\s\/\/.*$/`, `/(^|[^:])\/\/[^\n]*/`, `/\/\/.*$/gm`, a `(?<!:)` lookbehind — and `/^\s*\/\//` also appears in code that is not stripping anything). The durable close is probably the other direction: assert that a file which READS a source tree and scans it for a pattern imports the shared stripper, rather than trying to recognise every way of not doing so. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1034](../architecture/decisions.md). The spellings do not enumerate; the DELIMITERS do — three of them, each of which any comment-recognising regex must escape a slash in — so the guard keys on those, over source already blanked through the shared stripper, and falls from 118 source readers to 8 files with a registered reason. Building it found the gap had already cost something: `track_preview_mount_guard`'s own block spelling differed from the register's needle, and a `/*` inside an HTML comment blanked **906 lines** across five `.svelte` files while the guard reported a pass — § 971 recurring where its guard could not look. Same helper also blanked code points against UTF-16 offsets, misaligned by one emoji. Three further scanners converted; measured unchanged.
- [x] **The three API Lambdas still spell their own 405 where the five share ones now share one.** [§ 1005](../architecture/decisions.md) gave the share handlers a single `shareMethodRefusal`; coach, generate-route and osrm-proxy each still write the comparison, the status, the `Allow` header and the body inline, with the coach one going through a stream writer rather than a returned object. [§ 1006](../architecture/decisions.md)'s population guard accepts either shape, so nothing is unguarded — this is duplication, not a hole. Folding the three in wants a helper that can express BOTH the allowed-method set (POST for two, GET for one) and the two response shapes, which is a bigger change than the three-line saving justifies on its own; worth doing the next time one of those wrappers is opened for another reason. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1035](../architecture/decisions.md). Done properly rather than declined, because reading the three showed it was not only duplication: the share refusal sends `cache-control: no-store` and **none of the three API copies sent any cache directive at all**, so a 405 from `/api/coach`, `/api/routes/generate` or `/api/routes/osrm` was cacheable and would have outlived its own fix. `core/method_gate` takes the allowed set and returns the PARTS, which is what serves both response shapes — the coach's stream caller costs eight lines, nothing else changed shape.

## Surfaced by the #789 coverage round 34 — infra lane (2026-09-02)

Four filings closed in-round with their guards ([decisions §§ 1021-1024](../architecture/decisions.md));
two of the four were wrong about the fix before they were anything else, and
the corrections are in the ADRs. What follows is what this lane found and did
not take. This lane holds no AWS credentials by design, so every item below
says which half is verified from the repo and which is a claim about the live
edge, plus the one command that settles it.

- [x] **The Lambda execution role's `kms:Decrypt` on the secrets CMK is unexercised too, and emptying the statement is a structural change.** **CLOSED 2026-09-05 as DO NOT TAKE** ([decisions § 1267](../architecture/decisions.md)). The filing is factually right and its action is wrong: this grant and the entry below it are one architectural fact seen from two sides, and deleting the grant is the single thing that would make the plaintext-secret finding permanently unfixable. Every repair for that finding — a CMK on the function's environment, or a ciphertext env var the handler decrypts at cold start — needs the EXECUTION role to hold exactly this `kms:Decrypt`, which is what turns it from unexercised into load-bearing. Leave the statement, the variable and claim 9's restore knob alone. The live-configuration read the filing named is no longer what settles it. [§ 1021](../architecture/decisions.md) removed the deploy role from `AllowLambdaAndDeployRolesToDecrypt` and left the execution role, which by the same argument never uses it: `data.sops_file` decrypts at APPLY time and `local.lambda_env` puts the result into `environment { variables }` as plaintext, so the handler reads `process.env` and calls no KMS API — measured, no `kms` reference exists anywhere under `apps/web/lambda/`. The log-group encryption is done by the `logs.<region>.amazonaws.com` service principal under its own statement, not by the execution role. Not taken because `compact()` would then leave a principal-less `identifiers` list, which KMS rejects, so closing it means deleting the statement AND the module's `kms_decrypt_principal_arn` variable — removing the restore knob `scripts/check_infra_iam.mjs` claim 9 uses in the other direction. **Verified from the repo:** no `aws_lambda_function` sets `kms_key_arn`, so the CMK is not the env-var key. **Not verified:** the live function's own configuration. Settles it: `aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name threkir-web-prod-coach --query KMSKeyArn` returning `None`.
- [ ] **The deploy roles can read the production secrets in plaintext, and § 1021 does not change that.** **Analysed 2026-09-05, fix specified, not taken** ([decisions § 1267](../architecture/decisions.md)). It is **fixable, not inherent** — but the filing's own cost estimate is wrong by a factor of four and that is why it read as deferrable. Measured by walking every `*_lambda_env` local in `infra/modules/web-stack/main.tf` for a `data.sops_file` merge: **TWO functions carry a sops secret, not eight** — `lambda_env` (coach: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`) and `generate_route_lambda_env` (`GRAPHHOPPER_API_KEY`, `GRAPH_CYCLE_API_KEY`). The five share Lambdas and the OSRM proxy take public values only. The filing's premise is confirmed from `aws lambda update-function-code help` (aws-cli 2.36.4): the response carries `Environment -> Variables`. **Do NOT reach for `kms_key_arn` first** — `check_infra_iam.mjs` claim 9 holds "no `aws_lambda_function` sets `kms_key_arn`" as a live premise and, the moment one does, DEMANDS `kms_decrypt_principal_arn` be wired back to the deploy role, handing back the grant the fix is about; whether that demand is right (does `UpdateFunctionCode` need `kms:Decrypt` on the function's CMK, or return `Environment.Error`?) is a live API behaviour no lane can settle. **The route immune to that is a ciphertext env var the handler decrypts at cold start under the execution role**: `kms_key_arn` stays unset so claim 9 is untouched, `GetFunctionConfiguration` hands out a blob useless without `kms:Decrypt`, and the grant in the entry above becomes load-bearing. Cost: one `kms:Decrypt` per cold start on two functions plus a small shared module. Not taken here — unplannable without AWS credentials, six Terraform changes already unapplied, and it needs an edit to `scripts/check_infra_iam.mjs`. Owner trees: `infra/modules/web-stack/` + `apps/web/lambda/{coach,generate-route}/` + `scripts/check_infra_iam.mjs`. The sops values become plaintext Lambda env vars at apply time, and every API that returns a `FunctionConfiguration` returns them — including `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode`, which the release genuinely needs and calls eight times. So a `production`-environment GitHub Actions job can read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` by uploading the same zip and reading the response. The module's own claim-8 comment already says this half out loud ("visible to anyone who can call GetFunctionConfiguration") without following it to the deploy role. Closing it is not an IAM edit — it is not putting plaintext secrets in a Lambda environment at all: a fetch at cold start (Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store), or a ciphertext env var the handler decrypts, at which point the execution role's `kms:Decrypt` becomes load-bearing for the first time and the item above inverts. That is a design change with a cold-start cost, an availability dependency and a per-Lambda code change across eight functions, and it wants a decision before any code.
- [x] **`lambda:GetFunction` and `lambda:GetAlias` on both deploy roles are exercised by nothing.** Measured: the only `aws lambda` verbs any workflow runs are `update-function-code` and `update-alias`, and no workflow runs any `bin/` script — `bin/lambda-alias-sync.sh` is the one caller of `get-alias` and runs under the operator's own SSO profile. Same shape as the KMS grant [§ 1021](../architecture/decisions.md) closed. Filed rather than taken because it removes an unexercised verb without removing any access: the role reads the same `FunctionConfiguration` out of the `UpdateFunctionCode` it must be able to perform (the item above). Worth doing as least-privilege hygiene the next time `infra/github-oidc` is applied, together with a re-read of whether `lambda:PublishVersion` is required for `update-function-code --publish` or is a third unused verb — that one could not be settled from the repo. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1085](../architecture/decisions.md). All three verbs removed from both roles. **`lambda:PublishVersion` was a third unused verb**, settled from the request shape rather than from the repo: `--publish` is a boolean member of the single `UpdateFunctionCode` request (rendered by `aws lambda update-function-code --generate-cli-skeleton`, which prints that operation's own input model), `PublishVersion` is a separate operation the release never issues, and IAM models one action per operation. The durable half is `check_infra_iam.mjs` claim 10, which derives the verb set from the workflows' `run:` bodies and fails in BOTH directions — an extra verb is standing privilege, a missing one is an `AccessDenied` mid-release.
- [x] **The share Lambdas' 404 body is a single unstyled English sentence, and [§ 1022](../architecture/decisions.md) is what stops a reader ever seeing it.** `notFoundHtml()` in `share-entity` (and the equivalent in `share-run` / `share-route` / `share-recap` / `share-badge`) is `<p>This link isn't available.</p>` with a `noindex` — no styling, no navigation, no localization. It is unreachable today because the distribution replaces every 4xx body with the SPA shell, which is why the SPA's designed `.notfound-card` renders instead. The durable end state is for those handlers to return the SPA shell AT 404 themselves, at which point the distribution's 404 mapping becomes redundant and can go; the interim is correct but leaves five handlers carrying a body that is one config change away from being what a reader sees. `apps/web/lambda/` belonged to no lane this round. Handler half closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1036](../architecture/decisions.md). All five return `notFoundShell()` — the SPA shell through the existing `injectEntityHead`, so the same stripping that keeps a stale `og:*`/canonical/JSON-LD off a 200 keeps it off a 404 — and the `noindex` now survives whether or not the edge substitutes. It falls back to a minimal noindex document on an unusable shell rather than returning it unspliced (no `noindex`) or throwing into the outer envelope (a 503, the § 1004 defect). **The distribution half is still owed and is `infra/`:** with the handlers honest, `custom_error_response`'s `error_code = 404` block is redundant, and dropping it is what puts the `noindex` on the wire. Filed below.
- [ ] **Whether CloudFront decodes a path before behaviour matching is still unmeasured.** **The prescribed probe was run and CANNOT settle it — 2026-09-05** ([decisions § 1266](../architecture/decisions.md)). Two reasons, and the second is the durable one. (1) `preview.threkir.com` has no DNS record and never had one: `infra/envs/preview/main.tf:38` sets `aliases = []`. (2) Against prod the experiment is **degenerate**: `/api/%63oach/turn` and the plain control `/api/coach/turn` return byte-identical responses, but so does `/api/zzz-no-such-route` under both `GET` and `POST` — every path lands on the one substituted error body, so treatment and control are indistinguishable from a path matching nothing. No variant of the probe helps while that is true. **So this item is ORDERED behind § 1084's apply**, which is the change that lets an unmatched path answer differently from a matched one; until then the only thing that settles it is `aws cloudfront get-distribution-config`, i.e. a credential. Re-file the probe after the apply. Original filing below. [§ 1023](../architecture/decisions.md) added `URL_DECODE` to the three WAF scope-downs on a one-way-failure argument rather than on a measurement, which is sound for THAT change (it can only widen a rate limit) but leaves the underlying question open — and the answer decides whether an encoded spelling was ever reaching the Lambda uncapped. Settles it against preview, no prod exposure: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' 'https://preview.threkir.com/api/%63oach/turn'` — a 4xx from the Lambda's own auth gate means CloudFront decoded and routed it, a 403/404 from the SPA fallback means it did not. The same run answers the sibling question [§ 972](../architecture/decisions.md) left open about `OPTIONS` on the share behaviours.
- [x] **`terraform validate` passes on both env roots and on no module.** Run this round after every Terraform edit: `terraform init -backend=false` then `terraform validate` in `infra/envs/prod` and `infra/envs/preview`, both `Success!`, plus `terraform fmt -check -recursive` clean over the whole tree. What that does NOT cover is a `plan`: no lane has AWS credentials by design, so none of §§ 1021-1024 has been planned against real state, and the four changes are a KMS key-policy edit, a CloudFront `custom_error_response`, three WAF `text_transformation` blocks and one new module input at its default. The first is on a `prevent_destroy` key and is the one to read the plan for; the last is a no-op by construction (the module already received `""`). Apply preview first. Re-run 2026-09-03 by the round-36 infra lane after §§ 1084-1085: `terraform init -backend=false` + `validate` in `infra/envs/prod` and `infra/envs/preview` both `Success!`, `terraform fmt -check -recursive` clean over the whole tree. Still open for the same reason — no lane holds AWS credentials, so §§ 1021-1024 and now §§ 1084-1085 have never been planned. The two added this round are a `custom_error_response` deletion on the distribution and an IAM action-list narrowing on both deploy roles; neither touches a `prevent_destroy` resource, and the second is confirmed by the next release rather than by a plan. **Closed 2026-09-03** ([§ 1111](../architecture/decisions.md)) — re-run, and the re-run found a real gap that was not `validate`. `terraform init -backend=false` + `validate` in `infra/envs/prod` and `infra/envs/preview` both `Success!`, `terraform fmt -check -recursive infra` clean. The module still cannot be validated standalone (re-measured: `Provider configuration not present`, even though it declares `configuration_aliases = [aws.us_east_1]`), and its transitive coverage is now MEASURED rather than asserted — an undeclared-input-variable reference added to `modules/web-stack/waf.tf` fails `validate` in `envs/prod`, naming the module file and line. What was genuinely uncovered was `fmt`: the step lived inside the matrix job with a per-stack `working-directory`, and `terraform fmt` without `-recursive` reads one directory, so drift in the module was invisible — measured, all five per-stack steps exit 0 where a recursive pass exits 3. `fmt` is now one recursive job over `infra/` and `check_infra_coverage.mjs` reads the workflow's fmt invocations as scopes and fails when any Terraform directory falls outside them. Still no `plan` behind §§ 1021-1024 or 1084-1085 — no lane holds AWS credentials — so the standing verification item is re-filed below rather than retired.

- [ ] **The 403 -> SPA-shell mapping is distribution-wide, so every API refusal reaches the caller as `200 text/html`.** Measured on prod 2026-09-05 ([decisions § 1266](../architecture/decisions.md)): `POST https://threkir.com/api/coach/turn` returns **HTTP 200, `content-type: text/html`, the 5,666-byte SPA shell**, and so does `POST /api/zzz-no-such-route`. CloudFront has no per-behaviour `custom_error_response`, so the one `error_code = 403 -> response_code = 200 -> /index.html` block in `infra/modules/web-stack/main.tf` rewrites a 403 from ANY origin on ANY path. A client doing `JSON.parse` on a refusal gets a syntax error instead of the refusal, and a monitor watching status codes sees a success. **Both halves of the conflict are already documented and neither can move**: [§ 1022](../architecture/decisions.md) is right that 403 must stay at 200 because every dynamic client route is a missing S3 key, and [§ 1084](../architecture/decisions.md) removed the sibling 404 mapping naming `/api/coach*` specifically — the 403 one it left is the one that fires for an unauthenticated call, which is the normal case. So this is not a mapping edit: the shapes are a CloudFront Function on the API behaviours that suppresses the substitution, or an API origin that never emits a bare 403. That is a design choice with an availability and a cost dimension, which is why it is filed rather than taken. One thing to settle first, cheaply, once §§ 1021-1024 / 1084-1085 are applied: whether `/api/coach*` has a live cache behaviour in the prod distribution at all — from outside, a Lambda 403 rewritten by the mapping and an unrouted path falling through to S3 are indistinguishable, and `aws cloudfront get-distribution-config` separates them in one call. Owner tree: `infra/modules/web-stack/`. **The measurement is real and the named cause is WRONG — re-diagnosed 2026-09-06 ([decisions § 1307](../architecture/decisions.md)). Read that before acting on this entry.** `apps/web/src/lib/coach/handler.ts` returns **401** for an unauthenticated call, at two separate exits. Nothing on this distribution maps 401, so it passes through untouched — the entry's "the 403 one it left is the one that fires for an unauthenticated call, which is the normal case" cannot be right. The only 403 the coach path emits is the AI-disclosure consent refusal, which needs an authenticated caller with a profile row and is unreachable by the request that was measured; and the behaviour is not the explanation either, since `/api/coach*` has its own `ordered_cache_behavior` targeting `lambda-coach` with `POST` in `allowed_methods`. So the measured 200 text/html is **not** a coach 403 being rewritten — it is evidence the request never reached the Lambda, which is the issue #590 shape `main.tf`'s own comment records as proven once (only one of the two OAC grants, Function URL 403s before invocation, mapping rewrites it to the shell at 200, "the surface reads healthy while the Lambda never runs"). A stale prod bundle or a prod `/api/coach*` behaviour that does not match the repo read identically. **Every one of those is a live coach outage, not a body-format nuisance, and neither coach alarm can see it** — both key on Lambda `Errors` and `Duration`, which a request that is never invoked does not emit. The diagnostic gets CHEAPER, not more expensive: half the proposed `get-distribution-config` call is already answered from the repo (the behaviour is declared), and the half that matters needs no credentials at all — an unauthenticated `POST /api/coach/turn` that reaches the Lambda answers **401 with a JSON body**, so anything else is proof it did not, independently of the mapping. That is one `curl` against a public endpoint. The distribution-wide mapping is still a real design problem worth solving; it is just no longer the explanation for the one measurement behind this filing. Owner: whoever holds prod credentials, starting with the `curl`.

## Surfaced by the #789 round 34 firmware lane (2026-09-02)

Eight of the nine boxes this lane took are ticked in place above; these are what
it could not take, plus what the sweep for the same class turned up. The first
two are the same shape and the same reason: a wire field the phone also decodes,
so the firmware cannot move it alone.

- [x] **Widen `run_store::TrackPoint::ele_dm` to `i16` metres, the unit `CRS1` already chose.** **CLOSED 2026-09-03** ([decisions § 1026](../architecture/decisions.md)). The filed design was right and was followed exactly: `FORMAT_VERSION` 5, whole metres in the same two bytes, `MIN_FORMAT_VERSION` still 3, `ELE_NONE` still `i16::MIN` and unit-independent. Two things the filing did not name and this change added. The unit resolution is now a NAMED function on each rail (`run_store::ele_metres` / `eleMetresFromStored`) rather than a division spelled inline, because reading a v3 blob as metres is a silent tenfold error — magic matches, CRC matches, every field decodes — and the boundary is registered as `ELE_METRES_VERSION` / `kEleMetresVersion`. And **all three version bounds are now `CONSTANT_ROWS`**: `FORMAT_VERSION` against `_maxSupportedVersion` was the pair nothing could see, since this format flows watch->phone so the two halves are writer-and-ceiling rather than encoder-and-decoder, and each suite pinned only its own end. The metre is rounded rather than truncated, with the range test applied to the rounded value or a reading half a metre below the floor would round onto the sentinel. `record_cadence`'s ceiling-cost test is replaced by its inverse, `every_plausible_altitude_now_reaches_the_track`, which pins the NESTING of `plausible_alt`'s window inside the field's over all 9,501 metres of it — the hole re-opens from either side. Original filing follows. [decisions § 994](../architecture/decisions.md) measured the cost of the decimetre field — the ceiling is 3276.7 m, `elevation::plausible_alt` admits to 9000 m, and **69 % of a Silverton-Handies-Silverton profile stores no elevation**, with the summit push netting to zero vert because the gain rule carries the last reading across the dropout. [§ 334](../architecture/decisions.md) already made this exact decision for the course frame with the reason written down ("a decimetre `i16` caps at 3276.7 m, below Mont Blanc, and this is a mountain-ultra device"); the run track never followed, so the same watch can be handed a course it cannot record itself running. **The design, so it is not re-derived:** `FORMAT_VERSION` 5 storing whole metres in the same two bytes (`i16` metres spans +/-32,767 m — past Everest with 2x margin, and 1 m resolution is below both noise floors and below the 3 m gain gate); `MIN_FORMAT_VERSION` stays 3 and the unit resolves per header version, so **existing v3/v4 blobs stay readable with their original decimetre meaning** rather than being rejected or silently misread 10x high. `ELE_NONE` stays `i16::MIN` and `ele_dm_from_m`'s exclusion of it stays. **It needs a lane owning both trees**: `apps/mobile_android/lib/sim_watch_sync.dart` (plus its iOS twin) is the phone's production decode side — it reads the field as `eleDm / 10.0` and its `_maxSupportedVersion` is 4, so a firmware-only bump ships a watch whose runs the phone refuses outright — and the golden vector in `apps/mobile_android/test/sim_watch_sync_test.dart` that `scripts/check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs` pins moves with it. Half-metres were considered and rejected: metres match `CRS1`, and nothing consumes sub-metre altitude (`computeElevationGain` gates at 3 m, GAP now measures over 20 m).
- [x] **`RBK1` v2 for the per-checkpoint target time, so the wrist can show the verdict web has.** **CLOSED 2026-09-03** ([decisions § 1027](../architecture/decisions.md)). The design was right, and one of its predictions was wrong in a way that made the change smaller again: **no `CONSTANT_ROWS` row is owed for the band fraction.** The filing expected a second rail to acquire it, but under this design none does — the verdict is graded in `roadbook.dart` beside the builder that holds the band, `watch_roadbook.dart` only maps the already-graded verdict onto the wire, and the firmware deliberately never carries a threshold it never applies. The fraction stays held by the existing web<->Dart `roadbook` parity pair. What did land: a 19-byte v2 checkpoint carrying `target_elapsed_s(4) | target(1)`, both-or-neither (a time with no verdict, a verdict with no time, and an unknown status byte each refuse the whole frame — in Rust the pairing is a `CheckpointTarget` struct, so the half-present case is unrepresentable rather than merely rejected); `MIN_ROADBOOK_FORMAT_VERSION` 1 so an un-updated phone's v1 push still loads with no targets, since v1's CRC covers the same bytes and the layout is a strict prefix; golden vectors moved on both rails; and a `CONSTANT_ROWS` row for the checkpoint STRIDE, which is the thing a one-sided change would misread every field after the first checkpoint through while the CRC still matched. **And the wrist renders both halves**: a signed glyph per row beside the cut-off flag, plus the next target's TIME on the row below the window — a glyph with no number behind it is a claim a runner at hour twenty cannot check, and a wire field no page reads would be the § 24 mistake the whole entry exists to avoid. Original filing follows. [decisions § 997](../architecture/decisions.md) records why `roadbook`'s `RoadbookTarget` / `TARGET_BAND_FRACTION` is not ported, and it is a wire gap rather than a port gap: v1's checkpoint is `cum_dist_m | leg_dist_m | projected_elapsed_s | cutoff | flags` with the flags byte holding only `CHECKPOINT_FLAG_REFILL`, and `build_roadbook` — the ported builder — has no non-test caller, so the Roadbook glance renders only what is pushed. Closing it is: a v2 checkpoint carrying `target_elapsed_s` (a `u32`, 0 meaning none) and its verdict, the same shape the cutoff byte already has; `apps/mobile_android/lib/watch_roadbook.dart` emitting it, with the phone computing the verdict as it already computes the cutoff one (the proportional band is web's `TARGET_BAND_FRACTION` = 1 % with a 60 s floor, and it must be the phone's because a target is a per-marker `target_clock` / `target_elapsed_s` meta the watch never sees); the golden vector on both rails; and a `CONSTANT_ROWS` row for the band fraction once a second rail holds it. `route_markers::parse_target` is NOT needed on the wrist under this design — the meta stays phone-side, which is why the filing's "the input exists" premise was false in a way that also makes the fix smaller.
- [x] **`plan_replan` is missing `easeOffNextWeek`, and `segments` is missing three functions.** **CLOSED 2026-09-03** ([decisions § 1029](../architecture/decisions.md) + [§ 1030](../architecture/decisions.md)). The filing invited a read against the web source and the read found the premise half wrong and a live divergence underneath it. **`plan_replan` was not missing the ease-off RULES** — they were all present, inlined in `replan_remaining`, producing the same changes. What was missing is the reason web exports the function: its second caller. `plan_adaptive_replan.rs` implements web's P2 arms 1 and 3 and **omits arm 2**, the deep-fatigue deload override, along with `ADAPTIVE_DEEP_FATIGUE_TSB`, `ADAPTIVE_HIGH_ACWR`, `AdaptiveReason::DeloadFatigue` and `isDeeplyFatigued` — while its own header called the P2 gate "a faithful port". The omitted arm is the only one where the runner is at genuine risk, so a fatigued runner whose load said "bleed it off whatever the plan says" got nothing. `ease_off_next_week` is now extracted and public, both callers use it, and the override is ported with host tests. **`segments` split two ways**: `computeEffortsFromTrack` is ported and `build_segment_effort_rows` now batches through it as web's own caller does (the cumulative array and the median step are properties of the track, so the per-slice loop was 64 x (512 haversines + a 512-element sort) for an answer that does not depend on the slice — identical results, which is why nothing could notice); `computeGlobalSegmentEffort` / `_Efforts` are recorded as excluded in the module header, because they match against a free-standing catalogue geometry the watch holds none of and no frame delivers. A third finding on the way: `trend_code`'s doc comment has named a pinning test `trend_code_matches_discriminant` since it landed and that test existed nowhere, so the doc's argument about the explicit discriminants rested on nothing; it is written now. Original filing follows. Found re-running the [§ 899](../architecture/decisions.md) date comparison this round (14 of the original 16 pairs still show web ahead). `plan_replan.rs` exports one `pub fn` against web's two — the generator-v2 P2 surface the round-30 sweep named but did not enumerate. `segments.rs` exports three against web's six: `computeEffortsFromTrack` (the #733 batched walk, named in the round-30 filing), plus `computeGlobalSegmentEffort` and `computeGlobalSegmentEfforts`, which it did not. Each needs the same § 24 decision the five in that sweep got — port with host tests, or record the exclusion in the module doc — and neither module was read against its web source this round, so nothing here is a known divergence. `settings` shows the same date gap and is NOT one: web's five extra exports are `detectPlatform` / `deviceLabel` / `getDeviceId` / `dropUserCache` / `peekCachedSettings`, browser-platform helpers with no firmware analogue, plus two test hooks.
- [x] **The GAP window is 20 m on four rails and `roadbook` shares it on three, with nothing pinning that the sharing is deliberate.** **CLOSED 2026-09-04** ([decisions § 1159](../architecture/decisions.md)). Taken as the mechanised form rather than the prose one: `CONSTANT_ROWS` rows in `check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs` gained a `consumers` block — files that TAKE a value from the rail that declares it rather than restating it, each with the import that must match its source exactly once, plus the reason the sharing is deliberate. The roadbook's four rails (web, both Dart, firmware) are registered, and a guard test proves the failure: a `roadbook.ts` that declares its own window fails the check while every rail in the row still agrees with every other, which is precisely what nothing could see before. The reverse direction cannot be mechanised the same way — a reader retuning `MIN_SEGMENT_M` moves every rail together and the guard stays green — so the four GAP modules also carry one sentence naming the roadbook as a second consumer. Original filing: [decisions § 992](../architecture/decisions.md) raised `MIN_SEGMENT_M` after measuring that the shipped 5 m was below `ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_DELTA_M / MAX_GRADE`. `roadbook` imports the constant on web, both Dart rails and the firmware, so its effort allocation moved too — correctly, for the same reason, and its suites pass unchanged. What is not written down anywhere is that the two SHOULD share it: a later reader who decides the roadbook wants its own window has no note saying the sharing was a decision, and a later reader who tunes the GAP window has no note saying three roadbook rails move with it. One sentence in each `roadbook` module header, or a `CONSTANT_ROWS` `why` naming the second consumer. Not taken because the wording belongs in `apps/web/` and `apps/mobile_*` roadbook files this lane did not own.
- [x] **Nothing pinned the GAP window's value on any rail before this round, and the new pins are relationship-shaped rather than golden.** **CLOSED 2026-09-04** ([decisions § 1160](../architecture/decisions.md)). ## Surfaced by the #789 round 35 Wear OS / scripts lane (2026-09-03)

Three defects fixed in-round ([decisions §§ 1052-1053](../architecture/decisions.md),
[§ 1055](../architecture/decisions.md)), one item scoped and deliberately not
built ([§ 1054](../architecture/decisions.md)), one verified already closed and
six negative results recorded ([§ 1056](../architecture/decisions.md)). These
two are what the lane found and could not take.

- [x] **`avg_bpm` is saved as the run's average heart rate with no record of how much of the run it covered.** Falls out of [§ 1054](../architecture/decisions.md)'s scoping: `MeasureClient` is documented foreground-only, so on a twelve-hour ultra the samples that reach `bpmSum` / `bpmCount` may be only the minutes the runner spent looking at the watch — and `stopRecording` writes that mean into `QueuedRun.avgBpm`, which becomes the run's `avg_bpm`, with nothing anywhere saying it covered 3 % of the run. Not a `MeasureClient` bug and not fixed by moving to `ExerciseClient` alone: the same question would arise from a sensor that drops out. It became *computable* only with [§ 1052](../architecture/decisions.md) — the availability state means the recorder can now measure the seconds during which HR was `Available` and compare them to elapsed. Not taken in-round because the fix is a decision about saved data, not a wrap: either suppress the claim below a coverage threshold (changes what a completed run stores) or carry the coverage as a metadata key, which needs an entry in `docs/backend/metadata.md` and therefore an owner in `apps/backend/` as well as `apps/watch_wear/`. Decide the shape before writing it; the wrist half is small once the shape is settled. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1083](../architecture/decisions.md). **Both shapes, and both fit inside `apps/watch_wear/` plus the registry row** — the watch posts straight to Supabase, so no phone-side parser is involved. `metadata.hr_coverage` records the share of ACTIVE elapsed time the sensor delivered, and `avg_bpm` is suppressed below 0.5 because a mean over less of the run than not is not the run's average. Measured on the recording ticker against the AGE of the last sample, not by closing an interval on an availability event — a foreground-only client the platform stops feeding need never report `UNAVAILABLE`, and an open interval credits the silence. Null coverage is *unmeasured*, not zero, so a pre-field checkpoint recovers its average unqualified.
- [x] **`store.queue.first()` inside the drain is the residual of the class [§ 1055](../architecture/decisions.md) closed at the boundary.** That entry put a `.catch` on `store.queue` where it is *collected*, because a DataStore-backed flow reports a corrupt file by failing rather than by reading empty. The drain reads the same flow with `.first()` in `drainQueueLocked`, and `drainQueue` is called from eight sites, four of them inside `viewModelScope.launch` blocks with no guard — so an unreadable queue still reaches the thread's uncaught handler and kills the process the recording service is in. Deliberately not wrapped in-round: unlike the stream case there is a real decision underneath, namely what the drain should *do* when it cannot read the queue (report to the sync chip? back off? treat it as empty and risk a silent no-op?), and a blanket `catch` would pick the worst of those three by default. The broader shape is that `RunViewModel` has 23 `viewModelScope.launch` blocks and no `CoroutineExceptionHandler`; installing one on the scope would turn every remaining instance into a logged failure instead of a process death, which is probably the right durable fix and is a decision about the whole view model rather than about the drain. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1082](../architecture/decisions.md). Both rungs. Every one of the 23 `viewModelScope.launch` sites now goes through `launchGuarded`, which installs a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` that logs, and `ViewModelStreamResilienceTest` fails the build on a bare one. The drain's own decision is **report and back off**, not treat-as-empty: an empty read drains nothing, arms no backoff and CLEARS `syncError`, so the runner is told their runs are synced by the pass that could not open the file holding them. A `force` drain still gets through, which is what makes a retry after a reboot possible.

- [x] **`packages/run_recorder` needed `hide ActivityType` and only a compile caught it.** [§ 1013](../architecture/decisions.md) put `ActivityType` in `core_models`; `geolocator_apple` exports an `ActivityType` of its own (iOS's LOCATION activity type). `run_recorder` imports both, and `dart analyze` on either package reports nothing — only building a test that reaches `run_recorder` fails. That is a general hazard for any name added to the `core_models` barrel, and nothing sweeps for it. A guard that resolves the barrel's exported names against the exported names of every direct dependency of every package that imports it would catch the class; whether that is worth writing depends on how often the barrel grows. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1043](../architecture/decisions.md), as a measured **no**. **The filed premise is wrong**: the collision is an `ambiguous_import` ERROR at the use site, so `dart analyze` in the COLLIDING package reports it twice and exits 3 (reproduced by removing the `hide`), and CI's `Test Flutter packages` job already runs `melos exec -- dart analyze` over `apps/mobile_{ios,android}` and `packages/**`. Analysing `core_models` or the app reports nothing because the analyzer diagnoses only the files it is pointed at — which is what made the hazard read as invisible. The guard as specified would also be wrong twice: over the barrel's 115 public type-level names and the 48 direct dependencies of the six importing packages there is exactly ONE collision (`Route`, against `package:flutter`, harmless and already `hide`-handled), and `ActivityType` is not in that set at all because `geolocator_apple` is TRANSITIVE — it would have missed the case that motivated it. What was written instead: a note on the barrel saying where a collision surfaces and to analyse the consumers, plus `barrel_test.dart` pinning the two properties nothing else fails on (every `src/` library is exported; the package still has no Flutter dependency).

## Surfaced by the #789 round 35 backend/SQL lane (2026-09-03)

Three items closed in-round ([decisions §§ 1046-1051](../architecture/decisions.md)).
What follows is what the lane found and could not take, in each case because the
artefact lives outside the paths it owned.

- [x] **The export sweep's archives need a Storage-API reaper, and it is a Go-worker job kind.** [§ 1049](../architecture/decisions.md) measured what `cleanup_stale_export_blobs()` actually does: the `storage.objects` row goes, the archive stops being listable, and **the bytes stay on the storage backend with a matching `sha256`**. The sweep buys reachability, not erasure, and the SQL tier cannot buy more than that — a row delete is not an object delete, which is exactly why `protect_objects_delete` exists and why its hint reads "This prevents accidental data loss from orphaned objects." The durable shape is the one the closed entry named: a job kind drained by `apps/job_worker/`, which already writes the archive through the Storage API and already holds the service key, leaving `expire_stale_export_jobs()` as the only SQL half. It was not built in the backend lane because the enqueue needs a new value in `jobs_kind_chk` — a **set-shaped** CHECK, so `apps/web/scripts/check_constraint_unions.mjs`'s coverage rule demands a `PAIRS` edit naming every client rail, and that script was outside the lane. So this needs a change owning `apps/job_worker/` **and** `apps/web/scripts/`. Two design notes for whoever takes it, both from § 1049. First, the sweep currently destroys the only record of which blobs need erasing: once the row is gone nothing in the database knows the object exists, so an API-based reaper has to either run BEFORE the row delete or list the bucket. Enqueue-then-delete in one transaction is the cheap ordering. Second, a backlog table was considered and refused rather than half-built — an object name embeds a user id, so a table holding it after that user's row is deleted needs its own retention answer and its own interaction with `delete-account`, which is the same owner call as the payout-style gates. A queue nothing drains is worse than an honest gap. **Go half closed 2026-09-03; the SQL half is filed below and is one commit** ([§ 1112](../architecture/decisions.md)). `handler_export_blob_reap.go` + `SupabaseClient.ListStorageObjectsWithMeta` / `DeleteStorageObjects` + 15 tests are on `main`. The design differs from the filing's on one point and it removes the ordering problem rather than sequencing around it: the reaper LISTS the bucket instead of being handed paths, and since the list API reads the same `storage.objects` rows, the API delete removes bytes and rows together and the SQL row-delete becomes redundant rather than something the Go half must run before. An object the list API did not date is skipped, not erased; a non-positive `retention_days` falls back to the default; the default window is the SQL sweep's own 7 days and a test fails if they diverge. NOT in `Worker.dispatch` — `worker_dispatch_coverage_test.go` fails a `case` for a kind `jobs_kind_chk` forbids, and that CHECK is a migration this lane could not land.
- [x] **`docs/compliance/data-subject-rights.md` was corrected by a lane that does not own `docs/compliance/`.** **CLOSED 2026-09-04** ([decisions § 1136](../architecture/decisions.md)) — **the correction is right and stands**, re-read claim by claim against the code rather than against the filing: the sweep deletes `storage.objects` rows, `protect_objects_delete` exists because a row delete is not an object delete, the probe's bytes stayed with a matching `sha256`, `20260927_001`'s background-sweeper belief is unsupported, the Storage-API delete does remove the file (which is `delete-account`'s path), and the residual is that the measurement was on the local `file` backend. No retraction owed. **One sentence had gone stale and is fixed**: it called the durable fix "filed with an owner", and [§ 1112](../architecture/decisions.md) has since WRITTEN it — but `export_blob_reap` ships unroutable (`jobs_kind_chk` forbids the kind, nothing enqueues it, `Worker.dispatch` carries no case), so the state the paragraph describes is still the state in production. Both `data-subject-rights.md` and `retention.md` now say the fix is half built and inert and name the four statements that finish it. **One thing was missing rather than wrong** and is added: a Storage-API reaper cannot reach the bytes past sweeps already orphaned — it lists `storage.objects`, and those rows are gone — so the 74 files § 1049 counted stay on the backend whatever the reaper does. The `Status: scaffold` framing was not touched. Original filing below. [§ 1049](../architecture/decisions.md)'s measurement falsified the paragraph that said whether the bytes are reaped "is not measured here", and leaving a retention claim standing on a belief now known to be wrong was worse than editing outside the owned tree — so the backend lane rewrote that one paragraph. It is flagged here rather than hidden: if a compliance owner re-reads the file, that hunk is the one to check, and the surrounding `Status: scaffold` framing was not touched.
- [x] **The four filters are `> 0` now — and the branch the entry did not name could not save the run at all.** Closed 2026-09-03 ([decisions § 1078](../architecture/decisions.md)), migration `20270706000003`. The filed half is exactly as described and the four are tightened. The half it missed is reachable and worse: the **whole-run** branch has no positivity filter at all, and `runs_duration_s_check` is `duration_s >= 0` on purpose (a run imported with a distance and no time is a row we store, and `20270705000004` left it so). A zero-second run in a PR bracket is therefore storable, becomes the FASTEST candidate for that bracket, reaches `personal_records`, and is refused there by `best_time_s > 0` — from inside an AFTER trigger on `runs`, so the 23514 fails the INSERT of the run. Measured: an ordinary session inserting `(duration_s => 0, distance_m => 5000, source => 'app')` cannot record the activity, and the error names a table it has never heard of. So the entry's *"only a CHECK now stops it awarding a zero-second PR"* is right that the CHECK stops the award and wrong that stopping it there is harmless. The bound stays in the refresher rather than moving onto `runs.duration_s`: not having run 5 km in zero seconds is a PR-eligibility rule, not a storage rule. Pinned by `personal_records_positive_times_test.sql` (6 tests, each with its positive control). Original entry: `20270705000004` bounds `runs.fastest_5k_s` / `_10k_s` / `_half_marathon_s` / `_marathon_s` at `> 0`, which makes the RPC's own `and fastest_5k_s >= 0` filter equivalent rather than load-bearing — but the filter is still written in the shape that admits the bad value, four times, and a reader could reasonably conclude it is the guard. Tightening the four filters to `> 0` is a one-line-each change inside a SECURITY DEFINER body with a shipped pgtap suite over it; it was not taken in-round because the constraint is the root fix and re-emitting the whole function to change a comparison operator is a bigger diff than the defect justifies. Do it the next time that function is open for another reason. The same reading applies to `personal_records.best_time_s`, now `> 0` at the column.

### Surfaced by the #789 round 36 web / core + guards lane (2026-09-03)

- [x] **Four more script-end-tag regexes carry the `js/bad-tag-filter` defect, and three of them are production HTML sanitisers.** Found when CodeQL flagged the one copy [§ 1065](../architecture/decisions.md)'s split moved into `consent_guards.test.ts` — it reports an alert per changed FILE, so a byte-identical regex that had sat on `main` since it was written surfaced only because the code got a new path. That one is fixed. The siblings are not, and they are worse: `share/entity_spa_shell.ts:39`, `share/share_route_spa_shell.ts:50` and `share/share_run_spa_shell.ts:52` each strip an existing JSON-LD block with `<\/script>` and **no whitespace tolerance at all**, so a block spelled `</script >` survives the strip and the per-entity JSON-LD is then appended beside a stale default; `metadata_registry_guard.test.ts:113` and `:118` use the `<\/script\s*>` shape the fixed one had. The parser rule is that `</script` followed by whitespace, `/` or `>` closes the block and everything to the first `>` is junk, which `<\/script(?=[\s/>])[^>]*>` states. Not taken in the same change: three of the five are the served share-page sanitisers, and rewriting an XSS-adjacent production sanitiser at the tail of a five-lane integration, where it would get no review of its own, is the same argument [§ 1065](../architecture/decisions.md)'s filing made about moving a file mid-round. Owner tree: `apps/web/src/lib/share/`. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1086](../architecture/decisions.md). **The stated symptom was the small half.** Measured on the shells these files' own tests already use: against `</script >` the lazy `[\s\S]*?` does not stop, it runs on to the SPA bundle's own `</script>` and consumes the stale block, `</head>`, `<body>`, the `#svelte` mount div and the bundle tag — after which `injectEntityHead` searches for a `</head>` that is no longer there, takes its malformed-shell branch and returns the wreckage with none of the per-entity meta. A share page with no meta, no mount point and no application, not a stale node beside a real one. The search also found fourteen more of the same rule in the same files: every `<\/title>` (7) and `<\/head>` (5) closes the same way, `</title >` leaves the generic title standing for a crawler to pick and `</head >` drops the whole injection. 19 of the tree's 20 raw-text end-tag regexes were intolerant; only § 1065's own was right. The JSON-LD OPEN tag was widened too — it matched one exact attribute spelling, so a CSP nonce would have left a second `WebPage` node standing. `apps/web/src/lib/raw_text_end_tag_guard.test.ts` fails the PR on the intolerant shape anywhere in `src/` or `lambda/`, tests included. **Measured after the fix, which corrects the severity:** a production build's `apps/web/build/index.html` — the shell all five share Lambdas embed — carries a `<title>` from `app.html` and nothing else the strips look for: no canonical, no `og:`/`twitter:`/`description` meta, no JSON-LD. `SeoHead.svelte` spells its own close without whitespace and no `.svelte` file in the tree spells one with it, so the class was **latent everywhere, not live**. It is build output, so its bytes are a property of `app.html`, the adapter and whatever minifier is in the chain — which is the argument for stating the parser rule rather than matching today's emission. That measurement also turned up why the shell is so bare; filed separately below.

- [x] **The web/Dart geocoders are NOT a registerable parity pair, and the recommendation is that they stay unregistered.** Recorded so the question is not reopened as an oversight. The two modules diverge by design — web's `PlaceSearchOutcome` carries a third `aborted` state, web takes an `AbortSignal` where mobile injects a `GeocodingFetcher`, and web's geocode half falls back to Nominatim where mobile's returns null on an empty key — so a registry row would assert a lockstep that has never held, which is a worse failure than no row ([§ 604](../architecture/decisions.md) + § 641: the registry's value is that a row means something). What genuinely IS one contract is the pair of coordinate predicates, and the registry is keyed on module paths with no precedent for registering two functions out of a module. If a future change disagrees, it needs rows in BOTH the root `CLAUDE.md` table and `.claude/agents/shared-library-syncer.md` — neither of which a web lane owns, which is the same wall [§ 1014](../architecture/decisions.md) and § 1039's filings hit. Closed 2026-09-03 — [decisions § 1089](../architecture/decisions.md). Verified against both files rather than against this filing: all three divergences hold today, and there is a fourth — Nominatim rejects a stock HTTP-library User-Agent, so the Dart default fetcher sets one, and a browser forbids scripts from setting that header at all, so the two can never converge on one fetch layer. The `GeocodingFetcher` seam is also `Future<String> Function(Uri)`, returning a **body**, so there is no `res.ok` on the Dart side to mirror. Recommendation unchanged: no row, and the coordinate predicates stay unprotected rather than buying their safety with a standing lie about the other four differences.

The second is sharper: `snapToRoad` returns the unsnapped input point on a non-2xx and has no throwing branch anywhere, so no caller has a reason to wrap it. Both guarded, both pinned.
